tools.name: GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog (okf/ — the OKF spec + reference agent + viewer)
tools.one_line: The normative OKF home: SPEC.md (v0.2, 1003 lines), a Gemini+BigQuery reference enrichment agent, a Cytoscape.js HTML viewer, and 4 sample bundles — very active (created 2026-05-04, 174 open issues, 30 discussions), but it ships NO validator, NO releases and NO tags.
tools.notable: SPEC.md defines what lore must implement, including things a plain docs+graph CLI typically lacks: the Attested Computation concept type (§10: runtime, parameters, computation, executor{resource,receipt}, attester{resource} — a sanctioned computation plus a deterministic no-LLM attester so a consumer can prove the blessed query ran); the `sources` provenance family with per-source credibility signals (author, usage_count, last_modified) framed by a shared usage_window; footnote-label-to-sources[].id per-claim attribution (keyed, not positional, explicitly because agents reorder lists); the actor convention (<producer>/<version> | human:<id> | process:<id>) and DERIVED trust tiers (unverified / machine-confirmed / human-reviewed, never stored); status + stale_after (absolute date, not a TTL). Conformance §11 is deliberately permissive: only 3 hard rules — parseable frontmatter, non-empty `type`, reserved-file structure — and consumers MUST NOT reject on broken links, unknown types, unknown keys, or missing index.md. The shipped CLI (`reference-agent`) has exactly two subcommands, `enrich` and `visualize`; there is no `validate`. A recursive scan of all 405 repo paths found no validator, JSON schema, or linter for OKF anywhere in the repo.

tools.name: okfcli/okf
tools.one_line: Vendor-neutral single-binary Go CLI implementing OKF v0.2 end to end — the closest structural analogue to lore in the ecosystem, and it beat lore to SARIF output and a machine-readable CLI self-description.
tools.notable: `okf schema [command]` emits a complete machine-readable description of every command (flags, args, output format, exit codes) so an agent learns the whole surface in one call. JSON on stdout by DEFAULT (no --json flag), diagnostics to stderr. Structured error envelope {"error":{kind,code,reason,message}} with documented exit codes 0=ok / 1=validation / 2=io / 3=internal / 4=usage. Every finding carries a stable rule ID (okf/links/broken, okf/frontmatter/type-required) so CI suppresses or routes by ID, not message text. `okf validate --format sarif --exit-zero` emits SARIF 2.1.0 for GitHub code scanning. It deliberately makes broken links a hard exit-1 failure, which is STRICTER than SPEC §11 — a divergence lore should decide on consciously. Graph/backlinks follow §6.2 path-valued fields: sources[].resource, computation, executor.resource, attester.resource that resolve to concepts become derivation edges. Claims all four upstream reference bundles validate with zero errors. Repo tree confirms the enumerated surface (internal/{backlinks,bundle,concept,graph,index,initbundle,search,show,validate} + validate/sarif.go) with no mcp, diff, or context package; the 'Planned' list names only serve, render, and an okf-go library.

tools.name: serradura/okf-gem (`okf`)
tools.one_line: Ruby OKF toolkit positioned exactly where lore is — 'one durable home in your repo for the decisions an agent cannot re-derive from the code' — shipping Agent Skill + CLI/lib + graph server + MCP server + Claude Code plugin, but still targeting OKF v0.1.
tools.notable: Its README carries a positioning table (OKF bundle vs CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md vs agent auto-memory vs wiki) that is almost verbatim lore's pitch; the two rows it claims as its own are 'scales past one context window (progressive disclosure via okf index + search)' and 'checked by tooling (exit codes for CI via okf validate + lint)'. Verbs: validate, lint, loose, search, index, dirs, catalog, graph, stats, tags, types, files, render, server, registry, skill. `okf skill .claude`/`.agents` installs the companion agent skill; a Claude Code plugin adds a post-edit hook running validate+lint. A separate in-repo `okf-mcp` gem (lib/okf/mcp/{server,backend,registry,resources,output_schemas,filters,http}.rb with prompts/consume.md and prompts/search.md) is a full MCP server with output schemas and cross-bundle integration tests. A per-user REGISTRY names bundles: `okf registry set ./docs` then `@docs` works from any directory, and a bare `okf server` hosts every registered bundle behind one hub. `okf render` exports the graph as one static self-contained HTML file; OKF::Server::App is a mountable Rack app. Ruby 2.4–4.0, 3 deps, no native extension. Important for lore's gate design: `okf validate` implements only the three §11 hard rules and explicitly does NOT fail on broken links ('Do not expect broken links to fail validation. They are warnings by design'); `okf lint` finds them under reachability/backlog/provenance but exits 0 unless you pass `--fail-on warn`. Docs at okfgem.com, live demo, ghcr.io image, on RubyGems.

tools.name: scaccogatto/okf-skills
tools.one_line: The de-facto OKF v0.2 conformance checker in the wild (a single dependency-light Python script) wrapped as a Claude Code plugin, a skills.sh package and a reusable GitHub Action — the most-starred OKF-specific toolkit and the only one that was v0.2-throughout while the ecosystem was still on v0.1.
tools.notable: I read the validator source (skills/validate/scripts/okf_validate.py): it implements check_concept, check_computation (§10 Attested Computation), check_actor (§7), check_instant, check_trust (§5.2), check_lifecycle (§5.4-5.5), check_window, check_sources (§5.1 incl. footnote-label join keys), check_index (§8), check_log (§9) and check_links (§6.1). Broken cross-links are warnings by default ('tolerated under §6.1') and become fatal under --strict; --max-warnings N is a ratchet for gating CI while warnings are outstanding. Flags: --strict --max-warnings N --migrate --json. `--migrate` performs an in-place v0.1→v0.2 upgrade, rewriting a `# Citations` body list into a `sources:` frontmatter block. Ships as a composite GitHub Action (uses: scaccogatto/okf-skills@v1 with bundle/strict/max-warnings inputs) usable in repos with no agent at all. The visualizer computes trust tier and staleness at RENDER time and stores neither, with the rationale 'a stored tier is a stored opinion, and it goes stale'. Repo dogfoods OKF in .okf/ and CI validates that bundle on every push. Concept deep links (viz.html#services/auth-api).

tools.name: travisjakel/okf-ingest (+ sibling travisjakel/okf-mcp)
tools.one_line: The deepest OKF consume-side implementation: a byte-deterministic, LLM-free engine that loads a bundle into a portable DuckDB catalog, with a five-language conformance suite (R, Python, Rust, C++, MATLAB) locked to shared golden fixtures — low stars, high substance.
tools.notable: The single closest competitor to lore's context/impact/snapshot verb family, and it argues lore's own thesis back at it. Verb chain: validate → ingest → query → context → render (html/graph/export --mermaid) → impact → rank → doctor → diff → embed → rag, with --incremental and dir/git/tar/zip sources. `okf context` is the index-first, no-embeddings context primitive: index.md plus a concept's most relevant neighbourhood as one curated markdown blob ranked by EXACT Personalized PageRank over the author-written link graph (rank='bfs' for plain depth), or lexically-seeded multi-PPR when given a free-text query instead of a start node. `okf diff` reports drift since load (a snapshot changelog) and the MCP okf_diff/okf_refresh pair is framed as 'an agent's memory-refresh between looks'. `okf_sql` exposes read-only SELECT over okf_concept, okf_link, okf_validation. `okf_doctor` gives a health score plus per-rule findings with --fix. Resolves [[wikilinks]] by name (id/alias/title/stem) so links survive renames. Determinism is stated as a design line — 'the same bundle in always produces the same catalog, graph, clusters and HTML out, byte-for-byte, no network, no API key… There are no LLM agents anywhere in it' — with a parity test locking R and Python to byte-identical catalogs and ingested_at overridable so conformance stays byte-stable. Its README carries the ecosystem's only cross-tool comparison table. On PyPI (okf-ingest, okf-mcp), R-universe and crates.io. Self-described 'stable · lightly maintained'; authoring (new/add) deliberately not implemented.

tools.name: jyjeanne/okf-rs
tools.one_line: Rust tree-sitter code-to-OKF generator for 11 languages that emits a conformant v0.2 bundle as the artifact (not a SQLite index), with graph queries, git-ref impact analysis, a PR-review gate and an MCP server.
tools.notable: Its stated design property is one lore should steal the framing of: 'being wrong in public' — because the bundle IS the artifact rather than a binary index, a mis-resolved edge shows up as a red line in a PR diff to a reviewer who has never run the tool. `generate --check-determinism` verifies byte-identical output directly rather than asserting it in prose. `okf-rs impact <ref-a> <ref-b>` computes blast radius (every transitively affected concept), public-API membership and call-cycle membership between two git refs without touching the working tree; `okf-rs review <ref-a> <ref-b>` renders that as a sticky-comment-ready markdown report with --fail-on-risk merge gating and a ready-made GitHub Action. Graph queries: callers/callees, cycle detection, isolated concepts, cross-module deps, shortest call path, topology stats, modularity-based community detection. Validation covers the v0.2 generated/verified/sources/status/stale_after families and root okf_version, plus dangling links, redundant links, orphans, duplicate identity (path collisions AND same-symbol-different-file) and bundle-wide Calls/CalledBy symmetry. `okf-rs explore <query>` is a one-call context bundle (signature + description + callers + callees + blast radius), also an MCP tool, explicitly to avoid composing several search/graph calls. `okf-rs init` idempotently writes CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md / copilot-instructions.md with CLAUDE.md as a thin @AGENTS.md import. `okf-rs docs` renders static HTML, one consolidated MD, PDF, GraphML or an Obsidian vault — no LLM. Optional --lsp disambiguation via the project's real language server; optional `search --semantic` via any OpenAI-compatible /embeddings endpoint. Incremental content-hash cache and a watch mode. GitHub API reports Apache-2.0; the README badge says MIT OR Apache-2.0.

tools.name: openknowledge-sh/openknowledge (`okn`)
tools.one_line: Go CLI plus npm package badged OKF v0.2 with the broadest command surface in the ecosystem (27 documented commands incl. mcp, export, connect, automation, deploy) — but it phones home: telemetry is enabled by default.
tools.notable: Commands verified from the in-repo docs tree: agent, ast, automation, connect, deploy, disconnect, export, get, help, index, insights, jobs, list, mcp, prompt, registry, review, rules, runtime, scaffold, search, setup, spec, telemetry, validate, version, view. Two ideas worth noting for lore: (1) `okn setup --prompt` GENERATES the agent task text and declares 'the generated task is the source of truth for the setup workflow' — the CLI writes the prompt rather than the docs telling the agent what to type; `okn setup --agent <codex|claude|opencode>` then launches the runtime and finishes with `okn validate` + `okn setup complete`. (2) `okn scaffold` is called out as the DETERMINISTIC bundle-creation path, cleanly separated from `okn agent`. `okn export html` emits a static viewer plus an llms.txt, a connect manifest and a portable source archive — i.e. it treats llms.txt as an export target, not a rival. Publication is opt-in per file via okf_publish:false configured in Wiki/.openknowledge.toml. Install via curl https://openknowledge.sh/install | bash or npm i -g @openknowledge-sh/openknowledge. Telemetry is on by default (--no-telemetry opts out) — a hard differentiator against a strictly-local lore.

tools.name: gsemet/okf-schema
tools.one_line: The only OKF tool that adds real per-type JSONSchema validation — and it openly admits this makes it non-conformant, since OKF forbids a type registry and requires tolerating unknown keys.
tools.notable: Directly relevant to any lore decision to add typed frontmatter: schemas live INSIDE the bundle under `_schema/`, and the concept's `type` selects the schema file (type: tool → _schema/tool.schema.json). Accepts .schema.yaml, .schema.json and .schema.json5 (comments, trailing commas), with $ref composition. The README carries an explicit IMPORTANT block quoting SPEC §4.1 back at itself and conceding that requiring registered types 'is not allowed in OKF specification' — a good precedent for documenting a deliberate strict-superset divergence honestly. Also: bundle integrity checks (broken internal links, missing index.md, malformed log.md, reserved-file violations); comment-preserving frontmatter normalization via ruamel.yaml; auto-maintained `links`/`backlinks` frontmatter derived from body content; and standalone-markdown validation with no bundle at all. Commands seen: init, index. On PyPI, docs on readthedocs, CI + codecov + mypy.

tools.name: iwe-org/iwe
tools.one_line: Mature Rust markdown knowledge-graph engine (LSP + CLI + MCP, 20k files under a second) that predates OKF and has since bolted it on — `iwe init --okf`, `iwe schema validate`, `iwe find --filter '{type: …}'`.
tools.notable: The most important idea here for a tool agents WRITE through: `expect` guards. Every mutation must declare how many documents and blocks it may touch; the whole update validates before anything is written and aborts naming the offending blocks on mismatch — and over MCP the guards are MANDATORY, so 'an edit that won't declare its blast radius is refused'. Also: per-type document schemas (required fields, enums, ISO dates, required sections) enforced on MCP writes and on demand via `iwe schema validate`; mutations surface graph-hygiene warnings for the dangling links and orphans they disturbed; `iwe stats similarity` flags near-duplicates. Distinguishes 'inclusion links' (a link alone on a line = structural nesting, so one note can have multiple parents without duplication) from inline cross-references — a richer edge model than OKF's deliberately untyped links. Retrieval is `iwe find --fuzzy` → `iwe retrieve --key X --expand-includes 2` → `iwe tree --key`, with parent context included. Explicitly positions against putting memory in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md. Editor LSP for VS Code/Neovim/Zed/Helix; MCP server is `iwec` with file watching. On crates.io.

tools.name: langchain-ai/openwiki
tools.one_line: By far the largest OKF producer by reach — LangChain's agent-written codebase-wiki CLI emits OKF v0.1 output — and simultaneously the loudest evidence that the volume winner in this space is LLM-authored, not deterministic.
tools.notable: OKF support is real code, not a README claim — GitHub code search returns src/okf/frontmatter.ts, src/okf/index-sync.ts, src/okf/index-labels.ts, src/agent/okf-middleware.ts and test/agent/prompt-okf.test.ts (25 hits in-repo). The README states 'Open Knowledge Format (OKF v0.1) output with validated Mermaid diagrams'. Built on LangChain's Deep Agents and needs one of 12 model providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Gemini, Copilot, any OpenAI-compatible gateway), so it is the polar opposite of lore's deterministic bet. Two modes: code (repo → openwiki/) and personal (connectors → ~/.openwiki/wiki). Self-maintaining via ready-made GitHub Actions / GitLab CI / Bitbucket Pipelines templates that open a docs PR on every change — the update loop is a PR, not a diff command. `openwiki visualize` serves a loopback node graph with a side-by-side markdown reader, but loads its graph/markdown/diagram libraries from a public CDN, so it is not offline. Consumes MCP (Custom MCP connector, hosted Notion MCP) rather than serving it. .openwikiignore, --language <locale>, LangSmith trace connector for code wikis. On npm as `openwiki`. If lore needs one number for 'is the OKF bet lonely', this repo is it: 14,956 stars on an OKF producer.

tools.name: open-doc-spec/ods (Open Document Spec)
tools.one_line: A rival repo-resident markdown-doc-graph spec with its own Rust CLI that has absorbed OKF v0.2 as a flag (`ods lint --okf`, `ods init --okf`) — the clearest sign OKF is becoming a dialect other specs interoperate with rather than a standard they replace.
tools.notable: The sharpest competitive read on OKF's scope. ODS ships docs/other-specs/frontmatter-keys-ods-vs-okf.md drawing the line lore needs an answer to: use ODS 'when docs describe SOFTWARE SYSTEMS (services, guides, RFCs, APIs)… typed graph edges (depends, related) and code bindings'; use OKF 'when docs describe DATA/KNOWLEDGE ASSETS (tables, metrics, playbooks)… trust signals and staleness'. If that framing sticks, an OKF-native CLI for a code repo is arguably fighting the spec's grain. Features lore lacks: `ods mv <src> <dst>` atomically renames while rewriting graph dependencies, relative body links AND code references; `ods context <doc-id>` computes a bounded deterministic reading list in <5ms following depends: + context.load rather than dumping the repo, with a claimed ~95% token saving measured by `ods bench` (token ROI as a command); `ods adopt <dir>` scans legacy non-ODS markdown and drafts frontmatter as status: draft; `ods diff [target]` compares graph deps and frontmatter against git commits/branches; `ods lint --format sarif` (OASIS SARIF 2.1.0 → GitHub Security tab); `ods setup --git-hooks` installs a pre-commit link check; `ods stats` reports a health score, dependency density and profile distribution; `ods pack` / `share: private` exports sanitized public packs; `ods lsp` for editors plus a background FS-watcher daemon; `ods skill install` + `ods agents sync`. Custom profiles registered in ods.toml enforce expected_keys and H2/H3 section hierarchies and export as JSON Schema. OKF strictness is tunable ([specs.okf] check_keys=false, --skip-frontmatter-keys, --ignore-keys). Very low stars but shipped and CI-gated, with a GitHub Marketplace action.

tools.name: AnswerDotAI/llms-txt (llms.txt)
tools.one_line: Not a competitor — a different layer: one flat markdown index file at a WEBSITE root, no frontmatter, no typing, no graph; OKF tooling already treats it as an export target rather than a rival.
tools.notable: Verified from llmstxt.org: the structure is an H1 (the only required element), an optional blockquote summary, optional prose, then H2-delimited sections of `[name](url): optional notes` file lists; a file covers URLs under its path and the most specific applies. The spec EXPLICITLY rejects YAML frontmatter, using pure markdown conventions — so there is no `type`, no trust family, no provenance and no concept graph to traverse. Its scope is site-to-agent publishing, not repo-resident knowledge, and its only overlap with lore is context-window economy. Concretely non-rivalrous in practice: `okn export html` (openknowledge) writes an llms.txt INTO its published bundle, and modelcontextprotocol.io instructs agents to fetch its own llms.txt as a documentation index — which is the pattern's real deployed use.

tools.name: Model Context Protocol — Resources primitive
tools.one_line: A transport primitive, not a knowledge format — URI-addressed blobs with five metadata fields and no schema, graph, provenance or validation; every serious OKF tool serves MCP rather than competing with it.
tools.notable: Verified against spec revision 2026-07-28. A Resource carries exactly uri, name, title?, description?, icons?, mimeType?, size? plus optional annotations audience (user|assistant), priority (0.0–1.0) and lastModified (ISO 8601). Methods: resources/list (paginated, cacheable, with ttlMs/cacheScope), resources/read (may return multiple contents, may return InputRequiredResult for multi-round-trip) and resources/templates/list (RFC 6570 URI templates with completion-API argument autocomplete). Change signalling is notifications/resources/list_changed plus per-URI subscriptions/listen → notifications/resources/updated — a change PING with no payload, so a client must re-read; that is materially weaker than a diff verb and is exactly why okf-mcp had to build okf_diff on top. Errors are JSON-RPC -32602/-32603 (accept legacy -32002), not process exit codes. annotations.priority is the only context-budgeting affordance and it is a hint, not a budget. Two details lore should note: MCP defines a git:// standard URI scheme, and servers MUST sanitize file:// paths against traversal. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION.

tools.name: agentsmd/agents.md (AGENTS.md)
tools.one_line: The highest-star convention in the space and the real incumbent lore displaces — a single flat instructions file with no frontmatter, no graph and no tooling; its spec repo has not been pushed in 5 months (stale as of 2026-08-12).
tools.notable: Worth carrying in the landscape because two independent competitors argue against it in exactly lore's terms — the strongest available evidence that the framing lands. okf-gem's comparison table scores CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md as '⚠️ per-harness conventions' for portability, '❌ prose' for typed/queryable, '❌ loaded whole' for scaling past one context window and '❌' for checked-by-tooling. IWE says it more bluntly: 'Instructions are rules; memory is what builds up: decisions, corrections, the state of everything in flight. Kept in one flat file, the agent appends, contradictions pile up side by side each looking authoritative, and every session re-reads the whole thing.' Note the interoperation pattern several tools converge on rather than fighting it: okf-rs `init` writes generated content into AGENTS.md and makes CLAUDE.md a one-line @AGENTS.md import; ODS ships `ods agents sync`. AGENTS.md is a distribution surface for lore, not a rival format.

tools.name: Backlog.md
tools.one_line: Git-native markdown task/doc/decision tracker; npm `backlog.md` latest is 1.50.1 (published 2026-08-10), and it does have stable versioned `--json` plus a 20-tool MCP server — verified by running 1.49.3 locally, not from docs.
tools.notable: VERSION: npm dist-tag latest = 1.50.1 (2026-08-10); the locally installed binary is genuine upstream 1.49.3 from npm (platform-specific optionalDependencies backlog.md-darwin-arm64 etc.), NOT a fork — so every observation below is upstream behavior. JSON: `--json` is upstream and README-documented as 'stable, versioned JSON', available on `task list`, `task view`, the `task <id>` shorthand, and `search`. Envelope is {schemaVersion:1, kind:"task-list"|"task-view"|"search", ...}. TASK SCHEMA (from `task view --json`): id, title, status, type, priority, assignees[], reporter, labels[], milestone, parentTaskId, ordinal, createdAt, updatedAt, path, description, dependencies[], references[], documentation[], modifiedFiles[], subtasks[], acceptanceCriteria[{index,text,checked}], definitionOfDone[], implementationPlan, implementationNotes, comments[], finalSummary. ON DISK: YAML frontmatter (id, title, status, assignee[], created_date, updated_date, labels[], milestone, dependencies[], documentation[], priority, ordinal) plus HTML-comment managed blocks <!-- SECTION:DESCRIPTION:BEGIN/END -->, <!-- AC:BEGIN/END -->, SECTION:PLAN, SECTION:NOTES, under backlog/{tasks,drafts,docs,decisions,milestones,completed,archive}/ with config.yml. MCP: `backlog mcp start` (stdio); probed handshake returns capabilities {tools,resources,prompts,logging} and 20 tools — get_backlog_instructions, task_{create,list,search,edit,view,archive,complete}, milestone_{list,add,rename,remove,archive}, definition_of_done_defaults_{get,upsert}, document_{list,view,create,update,search}. VALIDATION (empirically probed, exit codes taken without a pipe): invalid status -> exit 1; nonexistent dependency -> exit 1 ('The following dependencies do not exist'); nonexistent task view -> exit 1. CRITICAL GAP: `--doc docs/nope.md` is accepted with exit 0 — the documentation[] field has NO referential integrity, so task->doc edges are unguarded. Exit codes are binary 0/1 only, not differentiated per error class. `doctor` repairs duplicate task IDs only — not a docs/link gate. Search is a lexical fuzzy index, not semantic. `backlog agents --update-instructions` writes a managed-block CLI 'nudge' into CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md (preserving surrounding content) — instruction injection, not skill generation. Also ships `board`/`browser` (localhost 127.0.0.1 Kanban web UI), milestones, and `instructions <guide>` as the agent-loop source of truth.

tools.name: github/spec-kit (specify-cli)
tools.one_line: GitHub's spec-driven scaffolder (v0.16.2, 2026-08-10) that installs markdown slash-commands and templates for 30+ agents; the deterministic part is a JSON-emitting script layer, while all spec authoring and 'analysis' is LLM prompt work.
tools.notable: ARTIFACTS: `specify init` writes .specify/ (memory/constitution.md, init-options.json, extensions.yml) plus per-feature spec.md, plan.md, tasks.md, checklists from templates/{spec,plan,tasks,checklist,constitution}-template.md — all plain markdown, no frontmatter schema. COMMANDS (templates/commands/): analyze, checklist, clarify, constitution, converge, implement, plan, specify, tasks, taskstoissues. THE KEY STRUCTURAL IDEA: each command's markdown frontmatter declares a deterministic script triple — `scripts: {sh: scripts/bash/check-prerequisites.sh --json --require-tasks --include-tasks, ps: ...ps1 -Json..., py: ...check_prerequisites.py --json...}` — and the script emits {"FEATURE_DIR":"...","AVAILABLE_DOCS":[...]}. The script header explicitly says 'Minimal JSON paths payload (no validation performed)', so the JSON is a path contract, not a validation result. VALIDATION: none that is deterministic. `analyze.md` is a read-only LLM prompt ('STRICTLY READ-ONLY', cross-artifact consistency across spec/plan/tasks, constitution conflicts auto-CRITICAL) — it is a prompt, not a validator, so there is no CI-gateable check of spec artifacts. Python CLI surface is small: `check` (verifies which agent CLIs are installed — a tool check, not a spec check), `version`, `init`, plus commands/{event,bundle} and integrations/{_install,_migrate,_query,_scaffold}_commands. CLI JSON is narrow: only `specify version --json` and it errors with '--json requires --features'. Exit codes are generic typer.Exit(1). TRACKER COUPLING: `/speckit.taskstoissues` converts tasks.md into dependency-ordered GitHub issues, declaring `tools: ['github/github-mcp-server/list_issues','github/github-mcp-server/issue_write']` — LLM-driven, one-way, no ID round-trip back into tasks.md. MCP: consumes an external MCP server but ships none (code search for 'modelcontextprotocol' in-repo = 0 hits). SKILLS: yes — AGENT_CONFIG covers 30+ agents with dedicated integrations/ dirs (claude, codex, copilot, cline, amp, auggie, ...), and the CLI has skills_dir/resolve_active_skills_dir with a skills-mode invocation style (/skill:speckit-*). EXTENSIBILITY: .specify/extensions.yml declares before_<command> hooks with enabled/optional/condition fields.

tools.name: Fission-AI/OpenSpec
tools.one_line: The most deterministic competitor in this set — npm @fission-ai/openspec 1.8.0 (2026-08-05) ships a real Zod-backed validator with named rule codes, `validate --all --strict --json`, and a declarative workflow schema; the README badly undersells it.
tools.notable: IMPORTANT: the README documents almost none of this — these findings come from the published 1.8.0 tarball, so do not trust README-based summaries of OpenSpec. ARTIFACTS: openspec/ with specs/ (markdown requirements+scenarios), changes/<id>/{proposal.md, design.md, tasks.md, specs/**/*.md}, archive/<date>-<id>/, and a per-change .openspec.yaml (supports skip_specs: true). VALIDATION (the standout): `openspec validate [item] [--all|--changes|--specs] [--strict] [--json] [--concurrency <n>] [--type change|spec] [--no-interactive]` backed by core/validation/Validator with STABLE NAMED RULE CODES: REQUIREMENT_NO_SHALL, REQUIREMENT_NO_SCENARIOS, REQUIREMENT_EMPTY, REQUIREMENT_TOO_LONG, SCENARIO_EMPTY, SPEC_NAME_EMPTY, SPEC_PURPOSE_EMPTY, SPEC_NO_REQUIREMENTS, PURPOSE_TOO_BRIEF, CHANGE_NAME_EMPTY, CHANGE_WHY_TOO_SHORT/TOO_LONG, CHANGE_WHAT_EMPTY, CHANGE_NO_DELTAS, CHANGE_TOO_MANY_DELTAS, CHANGE_SKIP_SPECS_{CONFLICT,ACCEPTED,INVALID_METADATA}, DELTA_SPEC_EMPTY, DELTA_DESCRIPTION_EMPTY/TOO_BRIEF, DELTA_MISSING_REQUIREMENTS, GUIDE_NO_DELTAS, GUIDE_MISSING_{SPEC,CHANGE}_SECTIONS. It enforces a real invariant: a change with zero spec deltas is REJECTED unless .openspec.yaml sets skip_specs: true. WORKFLOW SCHEMA: schemas/spec-driven/schema.yaml (name, version: 1, artifacts[] each with id/generates/description/template/instruction/requires) + templates/{proposal,spec,design,tasks}.md — the artifact DAG is declarative data. COMMANDS: init, validate, schema/schemas, doctor (relationship-health surface), context (working-set 'agent brief' as JSON, human listing, or --code-workspace editor file), show, spec, change, store, archive, fork, generate, list, status, instructions, config/profile, completion, templates, install/uninstall, register/unregister, feedback, experimental. Flags include --json, --strict, --no-validate, --deltas-only, --requirements-only, --no-scenarios, --allow-unknown, --concurrency. tools.name: Graphiti (graphiti-core)
tools.one_line: Bi-temporal knowledge-graph engine for agents — the only tool here with true valid-time AND transaction-time on every edge; v0.29.3, actively developed, OSS core under a commercial Zep platform.
tools.notable: THE BI-TEMPORAL MODEL, PRECISELY (graphiti_core/edges.py:263-283). EntityEdge carries four datetimes forming two independent axes. Valid time: `valid_at` ('datetime of when the fact became true') and `invalid_at` ('datetime of when the fact stopped being true'). Transaction time: `created_at` (when the row was written) and `expired_at` ('datetime of when the node was invalidated', i.e. when the SYSTEM learned it stopped holding). Plus `reference_time` = the episode timestamp that produced the edge. EpisodicNode has the same split (`created_at`=ingest, `valid_at`=event time). EDGE INVALIDATION ALGORITHM (graphiti_core/utils/maintenance/edge_operations.py): (1) an LLM using the `dedupe_edges` prompt is shown EXISTING FACTS plus FACT INVALIDATION CANDIDATES and returns two idx lists, `duplicate_facts` and `contradicted_facts`; a fact can be both. (2) `_extract_edge_timestamps` makes a SEPARATE lightweight LLM call to fill valid_at/invalid_at from episode text, resolving relative time against the episode's valid_at as REFERENCE_TIME; skipped if already set. (3) `resolve_edge_contradictions()` — for each candidate, SKIP when intervals do not overlap (candidate.invalid_at <= new.valid_at, OR new.invalid_at <= candidate.valid_at); otherwise if candidate.valid_at < new.valid_at then `edge.invalid_at = resolved_edge.valid_at` and `edge.expired_at = utc_now()` if not already set. Note the two different clocks: valid-time end is stamped with the NEW FACT'S valid_at, transaction-time end with wall-clock now. Nothing is ever deleted. (4) OUT-OF-ORDER GUARD: candidates are sorted by valid_at and if any candidate.valid_at > resolved_edge.valid_at, the NEW edge is born expired (`resolved_edge.invalid_at = candidate.valid_at; resolved_edge.expired_at = now`) — backfilling old episodes cannot clobber newer truth. (5) `if resolved_edge.invalid_at and not resolved_edge.expired_at: resolved_edge.expired_at = now`. QUERY: `SearchFilters` (search/search_filters.py) exposes valid_at/invalid_at/created_at/expired_at as `list[list[DateFilter]]` (OR-of-ANDs) with comparison operators incl. is_null — so 'what was true at T' and 'what did we believe at T' are separate queries. SUBSTRATE: pluggable drivers — FalkorDB (MCP default), Neo4j, Neptune, Kuzu (pyproject marks the kuzu extra DEPRECATED: 'the upstream Kuzu project is unmaintained'), plus `falkordblite` embedded. MCP SERVER: 13 tools — add_memory (with bi-temporal `reference_time`), add_triplet (bypasses LLM extraction entirely), search_nodes, search_memory_facts (with valid_at/invalid_at range filters), summarize_saga, build_communities, get_episode_entities, delete_entity_edge, delete_episode, get_entity_edge, get_episodes, clear_graph, get_status. PROVENANCE: Episodes are the ground-truth root; `get_nodes_and_edges_by_episode()` / MCP `get_episode_entities` trace source->derived, and every edge keeps an `episodes` uuid list for derived->source. TYPING: Pydantic entity/edge types plus an `edge_type_map` in config.yaml constraining which entity types an edge may connect. NO CLI: pyproject.toml has no [project.scripts].

tools.name: cognee
tools.one_line: Self-hosted knowledge-graph memory platform whose local dev path is fully embedded (SQLite + LanceDB + Kuzu, no services) and which exposes a raw Cypher search type — but whose graph construction is unconditionally LLM-driven.
tools.notable: SUBSTRATE IS GENUINELY EMBEDDABLE: README — 'Local development stays fully embedded — SQLite, LanceDB, and Kuzudb — with no extra services to stand up.' Production graph backends: Neo4j, Neptune, and a Postgres graph store shipped as an explicitly labelled DEMO feature ('The production ready feature is available as a licenced product') — a real open-core boundary to note. Whole memory layer can run on one Postgres (pgvector + SQL session cache + graph). 21 SEARCH TYPES (cognee/modules/search/types/SearchType.py) including CYPHER — a raw graph-query escape hatch backed by cypher_search_retriever.py — plus TEMPORAL, NATURAL_LANGUAGE, GRAPH_COMPLETION_COT, TRIPLET_COMPLETION, CHUNKS_LEXICAL, and CODING_RULES (coding_rules_retriever.py — rule extraction, the nearest analogue to skill generation here). TEMPORAL IS NOT BI-TEMPORAL: temporal_retriever.py extracts a {starts_at, ends_at} interval FROM THE QUERY via an LLM call (`extract_query_time.txt` prompt), then calls `graph_engine.collect_time_ids(time_from, time_to)` to filter nodes by event time. That is one time axis (event time), LLM-parsed at query time — no valid/transaction split, no edge invalidation, no as-of belief reconstruction. ONTOLOGY = TYPED VALIDATION: cognee/modules/ontology/ with base_ontology_resolver, matching_strategies, and an rdf_xml loader — you can ground extraction in a supplied RDF ontology. API SURFACE: remember / recall / forget / improve (plus add, cognify, memify, prune, export, push, proposals, sessions under cognee/api/v1/). CLI: `cognee-cli remember|recall|forget`, `cognee-cli -ui`. MCP SERVER: deliberately minimal — three LLM-facing tools (remember, recall, forget) plus workspace/MCP-Apps tools (visualize_graph_ui, upload_file_ui, open_cognee_workspace, cognify_file, and list_datasets_json / list_dataset_data_json / create_dataset_json / get_client_info_json structured-JSON helpers). Per-dataset isolation via ENABLE_BACKEND_ACCESS_CONTROL gives each (user,dataset) its own Kuzu + LanceDB under `.cognee_system/databases/<dataset_uuid>/`. MCP sampling mode delegates completions to the host's model so no LLM_API_KEY is needed (embeddings still required). Ships an official Claude Code plugin hooking SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit/PostToolUse/Stop/PreCompact/SessionEnd.

tools.name: Mnemosyne (mnemosyne-oss/mnemosyne)
tools.one_line: The local-first outlier: one SQLite file, one pure-Python dependency, no services, no telemetry, built-in MCP server — and a ~200-line uni-temporal TripleStore that is the cheap deterministic version of what Graphiti does with LLMs.
tools.notable: SUBSTRATE: a single SQLite file — sqlite-vec + FTS5, with 384-dim float32 embeddings binarized to 48 bytes (MIB, 32x reduction) and Hamming distance computed inside SQLite. No ANN index, no external vector DB, no services. Hybrid scoring is a fixed formula: 50% vector similarity + 30% FTS5 rank + 20% importance. Explicitly 'No telemetry — zero tracking, zero analytics, zero cloud dependency.' DETERMINISM: store/recall need no LLM; LLM fact extraction is strictly opt-in per call (`remember(..., extract=True)`), as is entity extraction (`extract_entities=True`). TEMPORAL MODEL (mnemosyne/core/triples.py) — UNI-temporal, valid time only: table `triples(subject, predicate, object, valid_from NOT NULL, valid_until, source, confidence)`. `add()` auto-invalidates by UPDATE'ing `valid_until = <new valid_from>` on every open row with the same (subject, predicate) — the module docstring flags this as 'correct for facts like "user prefers X" later superseded' and a later comment records the bug it caused for multi-fact writes (`add_facts` silently invalidated each prior fact because the invalidation key is (subject,predicate)). `end()` closes an interval explicitly. `query(subject, predicate, as_of=...)` does genuine point-in-time retrieval via `valid_from <= as_of AND (valid_until IS NULL OR valid_until > as_of)`. There is NO transaction-time axis — you can ask what was true, never what the system believed. ARCHITECTURE: BEAM three tiers — Working memory (hot context, auto-injected pre-LLM-call, TTL eviction), Episodic memory (long-term, hybrid search), TripleStore (temporal KG). CLI: `mnemosyne mcp [--transport sse]`, store, recall, stats, sleep (consolidation), export/import JSON, sync (bidirectional delta sync with optional client-side Fernet/PyNaCl encryption — the sync server sees only metadata). Memory banks give per-domain isolation. NOTE ON THE NAME: 'Mnemosyne' is a crowded namespace — also rand/mnemosyne (Rust, Claude Code semantic memory, 76 stars, last pushed 2025-11-23, i.e. ~9 months stale), nianpangzhi233/Mnemosyne-AI-Memory (2 stars) and Janadasroor/pg-mnemosyne-mcp (3 stars, Postgres MCP memory + task tracker). Only this one is materially active.

tools.name: Cline Memory Bank
tools.one_line: Not software — a prompt methodology prescribing six markdown files in memory-bank/, with zero code, zero validation and zero automation; the closest thing to lore in shape and the furthest from it in guarantees.
tools.notable: Exact prescribed tree (docs/best-practices/memory-bank.mdx in cline/cline): memory-bank/{projectbrief.md, productContext.md, activeContext.md, systemPatterns.md, techContext.md, progress.md}, with a documented dependency hierarchy — projectbrief feeds productContext + systemPatterns + techContext, which feed activeContext and progress. Crucially that hierarchy exists ONLY as a PNG in the docs; it is not machine-readable, not queryable, and not checked. Delivery mechanism is copy-pasted custom instructions into `.clinerules/memory-bank.md`. Three natural-language 'commands': 'initialize memory bank', 'update memory bank', 'follow your custom instructions'. Explicitly: no CLI, no schema, no link checking, no graph query, no provenance, no exit codes — updates are manual or LLM-triggered and correctness is the user's responsibility. Task coupling is only progress.md ('what works, what's left, known issues') — prose, no IDs, no tracker. Context-window management is delegated to Cline's /newtask and /smol. THE STRATEGIC READ: Memory Bank proves enormous demand for repo-resident markdown project memory (it is one of the most-copied patterns in agentic coding) while providing none of determinism, typing, link integrity, or graph — which is precisely the gap a deterministic OKF docs+graph CLI fills. Host repo cline/cline is Apache-2.0, 66,089 stars, pushed 2026-08-13.

tools.name: zetl
tools.one_line: The closest direct analogue found: a Rust CLI that indexes a Markdown vault into a typed wikilink graph with a CI-gating check, jj-backed time travel, a defeasible-reasoning engine, an MCP server, and a self-installing Claude Code skill — self-described "alpha", 1 fork and 5 Codeberg stars, so near-zero adoption despite the deepest feature overlap of anything in this category.
tools.notable: Typed edges in Markdown: `predicate::[[Target]]`, chained `supersedes::informed_by::[[Y]]`, CURIE form `prov:wasDerivedFrom::[[X]]`, nested-bullet annotations; queried by `zetl edges --predicate/--by-predicate/--untyped/--annotated`, JSON `{source,target,predicate|null,annotation|null,line,is_ghost}`. Vocabulary governance via `.zetl/predicates.toml` (`enforce=true` makes an undeclared predicate an ERROR) plus emergent-drift lints `predicate-drift`, `predicate-prefer-conforms-to`, `predicate-relates-to-overuse`, `predicate-undeclared-prefix`. CI gate: `zetl check [--dead-links|--orphans|--syntax|--spl|--drift] --fail-on error|warning`. Time travel: global `--at "3 days ago"` on EVERY read-only command (jj-lib snapshots in `.zetl/jj/`), plus `history log`, `history page`, and `zetl diff --from <REF>|--since <DATE> --filter pages|links|orphans|dead-links`. Reasoning (`--features reason`): SPL (Spindle Lisp) in ```spl fences and `.spl` files; `reason status|explain|why-not|require|what-if|conflicts|export|provenance`; conclusion types `+D/-D/+d/-d`; `explain --format natural|dot` proof trees; `conflicts --fail-on-conflicts`; `provenance` traces to source file and line. MCP (`--features mcp`): `zetl mcp [--transport http --port 3100]`, 9 tools — `search`, `get_page`, `links`, `backlinks`, `path`, `similar`, `check`, `status`, `reason` — with `zetl delegate --tools search,get --scope "projects/**" --expiry 7d` minting user-signed scoped JWTs and `--allowed-issuer <DID>` on the server. `zetl skill init [--user|--global]` writes `.claude/skills/zetl/SKILL.md` from a copy embedded in the binary (agentskills.io frontmatter schema), so skill and CLI version together. Also: `blocks --type heading --resolve <BLAKE3-prefix>` content-addressable Merkle blocks; `export --rdf turtle|ntriples|jsonld --base-iri`; `watch --debounce --exec` streaming NDJSON graph events; `agent run --budget <TOKENS>`; `search --semantic/--hybrid` (`--features semantic`) and `--near <PAGE> --depth N`; global `-f json|table|auto` with auto-JSON when piped and `--no-input` for CI. SPEC-046 specs `zetl okf check/import` and `export --format okf` against Open Knowledge Format v0.1 — but it is an explicit strawman, "NOT converged", and absent from the v0.5.0 CLI reference.

tools.name: Foam
tools.license: NOASSERTION (GitHub API); the `@foam/cli` and `@foam/mcp` packages both declare MIT
tools.one_line: No longer just a VS Code extension: the monorepo now ships a published headless `foam` CLI (npm `foam-cli` 0.46.1, 2026-07-24) with `--format json` on every command, a documented exit-code table, and a 25-tool MCP server — the most credible mainstream competitor to a repo-resident docs CLI.
tools.notable: Documented exit-code contract that separates tool failure from content failure: `0` success, `1` command error, `2` issues found (lint/check) — "`2` is CI-friendly". `--format json` on ALL commands, and every JSON response carries the Foam short `id` (usable as a wikilink target) alongside `uri`. Commands: `lint [--fix] [--rule missing-heading|stale-definitions]`, `list notes|tags|orphans|deadends|placeholders|templates` (with `--type`, `--tag`, `--sort count`), `note show|id|create|move|delete` (delete goes to `.foam/trash/`), `outline`, `links [--incoming|--outgoing]` (alias `connections`), `daily [--create] [--path-only]`, `tag list|search|rename`, `grep --context --limit`, `search --tag --property status=draft --type`, `rename note|tag|section|block` with automatic wikilink rewriting workspace-wide, and `mcp [--allow-writes]`. MCP server (`@foam/mcp`, MCP SDK + zod) has an explicit required `mode: 'read' | 'read-write'` and 25 tools in six modules: resources (`list_resources`, `get_resource`, `read_resource`, `create_resource`, `update_resource`, `delete_resource`, `move_resource`), graph (`get_workspace_info`, `get_connections`, `get_orphans`, `get_deadends`, `get_placeholders`, `traverse_graph` — BFS capped at depth 5, `get_graph_summary`), tags (`list_tags`, `search_by_tag`, `add_tags`, `remove_tags`, `rename_tag`), search (`search_resources`, `search_by_property`), structure (`get_outline`), and saved queries (`list_queries`, `get_query`, `run_query` over YAML files committed under `.foam/queries/`). Typed MCP errors map `FoamErrorCode` — `resource_not_found`, `ambiguous_identifier`, `resource_exists`, `invalid_input`, `io_error`. Server is long-running and watches the filesystem (chokidar) so external edits appear in later tool calls. Gaps vs. a graph CLI: no shortest-path command, no dead-link lint rule (unresolved wikilinks are first-class "placeholders" by design, not errors), and no history/diff.

tools.name: Logseq
tools.one_line: Very actively developed and now ships a real headless CLI (npm `@logseq/cli` 0.4.3, MIT) with Datalog queries, a native task model, and `skill install` — but the CLI targets the DB version whose source of truth is SQLite under `~/logseq/graphs`, so you cannot point it at a repo's `docs/` tree.
tools.notable: `@logseq/cli` (binary `logseq`, built from an OCaml/Dune/Melange runtime in `cli/` driving a ClojureScript `db-worker-node` daemon). Native task tracker inside the knowledge graph: `list task [--status <s>] [--priority low|medium|high|urgent] [--fields <csv>]` over nodes tagged `#Task`, and `upsert task [--status] [--priority] [--scheduled <datetime>] [--deadline <datetime>] [--no-status] [--no-priority] ...` for pages, blocks, and existing nodes, with `--status` validated at runtime against the values in the current graph. `agent bridge` routes tasks to named agents and reports typed non-routability reasons `Missing_stable_uuid | Missing_task_tag | Not_todo | Assignee_mismatch | Already_routed`, with prompt templates carrying `required_vars`/`allowed_vars`. `query` runs arbitrary Datalog (EDN) with named `:custom-queries` (`:query`, `:doc`, `:inputs` with `:name`/`:default`) resolvable from config plus built-in rules from `logseq.db.frontend.rules`; `query --list` enumerates them. Real property schemas: `:property-type`, `:property-cardinality` (`:one`/`:many`), `:property-classes`, `:class-extends`, `:class-properties`; `graph validate [--fix]`; `doctor [--dev-script]` returns a structured `report` of `check` records with `Ok|Warning|Error` status. `skill show` / `skill install [--global]` writes `./.agents/skills/logseq-cli/SKILL.md` (or `~/.agents/...`). Structured output via `--output json|edn` (config `:output-format`), env-var and flag precedence layering, and keyword error codes (`graph-exists`, `remote-graph-not-found`, `graph-db-not-empty`, `invalid-options`, `sync-not-started`, `e2ee-password-not-found`) — but no documented exit-code table. Snapshots via `graph backup create|list|restore|remove` and `graph export --type edn|sqlite` / `graph import`, though no graph-level diff. Separate MCP server in the Electron app (`src/electron/electron/mcp_server.cljs`, "Logseq MCP Server") exposing 6 tools: `listPages`, `getPage`, `upsertNodes` (batch add/edit of block|page|tag|property with a `dry-run` validate-only flag), `searchBlocks`, `listTags`, `listProperties` — note it has no backlink or path traversal tool.

tools.name: Dendron
tools.one_line: Effectively dead — the README states verbatim "Dendron is currently in maintenace only, active development has ceased." (sic), the last `@dendronhq/dendron-cli` npm publish was v0.124.2 on 2024-03-10, and the only 2025 commit was adding a workflow file; still worth studying because its hierarchical schema system is the most developed typed-note model in this category.
tools.notable: Schemas are the standout: `SchemaUtils.matchPath` / `matchPathWithSchema` in `packages/common-all/src/schema.ts` match dot-delimited note hierarchies against declared schema definitions, giving typed, pattern-matched note namespaces — the nearest thing in this category to validating that a note of a given kind exists in the right place with the right children. `dendron doctor --action <a> [--dryRun] [--query] [--limit]` exposes a fixed action enum (`DoctorActionsEnum`): `fixFrontmatter`, `h1ToTitle`, `h1ToH2`, `removeStubs`, `createMissingLinkedNotes`, `regenerateNoteId`, `findBrokenLinks`, `fixRemoteVaults`, `fixAirtableMetadata`, `addMissingDefaultConfigs`, `removeDeprecatedConfigs`, `fixSelfContainedVaultsInConfig`, `fixInvalidFileNames` — so broken-link detection and auto-creation of missing linked notes exist as first-class repairable actions, though no documented non-zero-exit CI gate. `dendron note` CLI supports `NoteCommands` lookup/get/find/delete/move/write with `NoteCLIOutput` of `json`, `md_gfm`, or `md_dendron`. Other CLI surfaces: `doctor`, `publish`, `export/import pod` (+ `podsV2`), `seed`, `vault`, `workspace`, `visualize`, `launchEngineServer` (a headless engine server other tools can drive). Task notes exist as a typed workspace concern (`packages/common-all/src/types/configs/workspace/task.ts`, `plugin-core/src/commands/TaskStatus.ts`, `unified/src/decorations/taskNotes.ts`) with status decoration, but the task surface is VS Code-side rather than CLI-side. Note references (`![[note]]`, including partial-note embeds) give real transclusion.

tools.name: Quartz v4
tools.one_line: Very actively maintained and has a genuine CLI, but it is a publishing pipeline, not a knowledge-graph query tool — the graph, backlinks, and search all exist only as components rendered into the output site, with nothing to query from a terminal or an agent.
tools.notable: CLI is `npx quartz <cmd>`: `create` (template choice: default, obsidian, ttrpg, blog), `build` (with dev server), `sync` (GitHub push/pull), `upgrade` (alias `update`), `restore` (recover the content folder from local cache), `plugin install|add|remove|prune|list`, and `tui` (interactive terminal plugin/layout manager). Global flags `--directory/-d` (default `content`), `--verbose/-v`, `--concurrency/-c`. Structured output is limited to `build --bundleInfo`, which writes a JSON file of bundle sizes — there is no JSON envelope for content or graph queries. Broken-link handling is presentational only: the `CrawlLinks` transformer's `disableBrokenWikilinks` option adds a `broken` CSS class alongside `internal` on links whose resolved slug has no matching file, so they can be styled differently — detection exists, but there is no check command and no CI gate. Graph view, backlinks, explorer, breadcrumbs, popover previews, and full-text search are all site components (`docs/features/`), not queryable interfaces. Plugins have moved to a separate `quartz-community` org installed via `npx quartz plugin add github:quartz-community/<name>`. Code search for `modelcontextprotocol` across the repo returns 0 hits.

tools.name: org-roam
tools.one_line: Emacs-only and slowing (last commits 2026-04-25, mostly build/version bumps) — there is no CLI, no JSON, and no MCP server in the core repo, so it is a reference for the node/backlink data model rather than a competitor to a headless docs CLI.
tools.notable: The whole surface is Emacs Lisp — the repo root is `org-roam.el`, `org-roam-db.el`, `org-roam-node.el`, `org-roam-id.el`, `org-roam-capture.el`, `org-roam-mode.el`, `org-roam-migrate.el`, `org-roam-compat.el`, `org-roam-log.el`, `org-roam-utils.el` plus `extensions/`. There is no `bin/`, no CLI entry point, and code search for `mcp` in the repo returns 0 hits. Its one genuinely transferable idea is the cache: `org-roam-db.el` maintains a real SQLite database (via emacsql) of nodes, links, refs, tags, and aliases that is rebuilt incrementally by `org-roam-db-sync`, and is queryable with arbitrary SQL through `org-roam-db-query` — so the graph is a first-class relational artifact, not an in-memory view, and every node row records its file plus point/outline-path, giving file-and-position provenance for any node. Task coupling is inherited rather than provided: because org-roam nodes are ordinary Org headings, org-mode TODO keywords and org-agenda already operate over the same substrate as the notes, which is the tightest notes-and-tasks unification in this set — but org-roam itself contributes no task commands. Graph visualisation and any web UI are out-of-core (org-roam-ui and similar), which I did not audit.

tools.name: Diátaxis
tools.one_line: A documentation authoring framework, not software: four types on two axes, with zero tooling, zero validation, and no machine-readable artifact of any kind.
tools.notable: Prescribes exactly four types — tutorials (learning-oriented), how-to guides (task-oriented), technical reference (information-oriented), explanation (understanding-oriented) — positioned on two axes: practical/theoretical and specific/general (acquisition vs application of skill). Crucially it says it 'doesn't impose implementation constraints': the taxonomy is a *user-need* taxonomy, deliberately open, with no schema, no required fields, no relationships between the four types, and no way to mechanically decide whether a given page conforms. That is the exact inverse of a closed typed-concept system (ADR/Spec/Story/Runbook/Reference), which is an *artifact-lifecycle* taxonomy: closed set, per-type required frontmatter, typed edges between concepts, and machine-checkable membership. The two are orthogonal rather than competing — a Runbook is a how-to, an ADR is explanation, a Reference is reference — so lore can claim Diátaxis compliance as a *presentation* property while keeping its own closed set as the *validation* property. The observable gap Diátaxis leaves open, and that lore fills, is that nothing in Diátaxis is enforceable: canonical repo is github.com/evildmp/diataxis-documentation-framework (1192 stars, pushed 2026-08-07, license reported NOASSERTION by the GitHub API).

tools.name: Docusaurus
tools.one_line: The only tool in this set whose broken-link gate is on by default (onBrokenLinks: 'throw'), but its agent story is entirely community plugins — no first-party llms.txt, no MCP.
tools.notable: Front matter IS schema-validated: packages/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/src/frontMatter.ts defines `DocFrontMatterSchema` as a Joi object (id, title, hide_title, sidebar_position: Joi.number(), tags via FrontMatterTagsSchema, last_update, pagination_next: Joi.string().allow(null), …) run through `validateFrontMatter()`, so a wrong *type* fails the build — but the schema ends in `.unknown()`, so arbitrary extra keys pass silently and there is no user-definable content-type system. Breakage handling is split into three independently-configurable classes with different defaults, which is the design idea worth copying: `onBrokenLinks` defaults to `'throw'`, while `onBrokenAnchors` and `onBrokenMarkdownLinks` both default to `'warn'`; all three accept 'ignore' | 'log' | 'warn' | 'throw'. Versioning gives a point-in-time snapshot (`docusaurus docs:version 1.1.0` copies docs/ into versioned_docs/version-1.1.0/) but there is no diff command. CLI surface is start/build/swizzle/deploy/serve/clear/write-translations/write-heading-ids — nothing emits a graph, index, or JSON envelope. Provenance is presentational only (editUrl / custom_edit_url, git-derived last_update). AI: the changelog through 3.10.2 (2026-07-10) contains no llms.txt, llms-full, MCP, or markdown-emission entries; 3.9 (2025-09-25) only added Algolia DocSearch v4 with AskAI, a hosted third-party surface. MCP exists solely as community plugins (e.g. docusaurus-plugin-mcp-server); maintainers framed a runtime MCP server as out of scope.

tools.name: MkDocs
tools.one_line: Has the most granular per-diagnostic link-validation config of any tool here, but it warns rather than fails by default — and core is stale: last PyPI release 1.6.1 on 2024-08-30, last repo push 2025-10-20.
tools.notable: The `validation:` config is a two-level tree — nav.{omitted_files, not_found, absolute_links} and links.{not_found, anchors, absolute_links, unrecognized_links} — where each leaf is independently set to warn | info | ignore. MkDocs 1.6 defaults: nav.not_found = warn, links.not_found = warn, everything else info. That per-diagnostic severity dial, decoupled from a single global switch, is a better gate design than one --strict flag; the failure decision is then a separate axis (`strict: true` / `--strict` halts on any warning). Front matter is explicitly NOT validated: docs state MkDocs supports YAML and MultiMarkdown meta-data and that 'the key/value pairs are passed by MkDocs to the page template' — free-form, with only `template` and `title` having built-in meaning. Machine-readable output exists but is incidental: the bundled search plugin writes `search/search_index.json` at on_post_build (mkdocs/contrib/search/__init__.py) — a full text+anchor index of every page, consumable by an agent, though never presented as an API. No CLI JSON envelope; exit code is the only machine signal. Provenance is a single `edit_uri` template, page-level, no commit hash.

tools.name: Material for MkDocs
tools.one_line: Very actively maintained theme+plugin suite on top of a stale MkDocs core; inherits MkDocs' warn-by-default link validation and adds no agent-facing output — no built-in llms.txt plugin.
tools.notable: Built-in plugin roster as documented: management — group, meta, projects, info; optimization — social, optimize, privacy, offline; content — blog, search, tags, typeset. Two are structurally interesting for a typed-docs CLI: `meta` applies front-matter defaults to every page in a directory (a directory-scoped default-injection mechanism, though it validates nothing), and `projects` builds multiple MkDocs projects as one site (a multi-bundle composition primitive). There is no llmstxt plugin in the built-in set — native llms.txt is an open feature request (discussion #8384), and the ecosystem answer is the third-party pawamoy/mkdocs-llmstxt (ISC, 129 stars, pushed 2026-08-13). Link integrity, front-matter handling, and exit-code behaviour are all inherited unchanged from MkDocs core, so the same warn-by-default caveat applies. Search remains client-side keyword (Lunr-derived), not semantic.

tools.name: Antora
tools.one_line: The best machine-readable diagnostics of any OSS docs generator — JSON Lines logs plus a configurable failure threshold — but the threshold defaults to 'fatal', so broken xrefs log an error and the build still passes.
tools.notable: Separates diagnostic severity from build-failure policy — the single most transferable idea here. `--log-format` accepts json (JSON Lines, one valid JSON value per line) or pretty; `--log-level` takes fatal|error|warn|info|debug|trace|all|silent (default warn); and `--log-failure-level` independently takes fatal|error|warn|none to decide what actually fails the run. Default failure_level is `fatal`, so a broken xref — logged at error level with file path, line number and source — does NOT fail the build unless you opt in, making it a real gate only after configuration. Docs even show jq consumption: `antora --log-level error playbook.yml | jq 'select(.name == "asciidoctor" and (.msg | contains(" not found:")))'`. Provenance is genuinely per-page and commit-accurate: Antora computes {web_url}, {refname}, {reftype}, {refhash} and {path} for every page from its content source and file origin, exposes `page-edit-url` and `page-origin-private` as intrinsic attributes, and can read from linked git worktrees. Graph access is programmatic, not CLI: extensions get a `contentCatalog` with getComponents(), getComponentVersion(name, version), findBy(query), getPages(filter), resolvePage(spec, context) and addFile(), and can walk pages, navigation trees and file families (pages/attachments/partials). Multi-version by construction (component versions from git branches/tags) but no diff command. Hosted on GitLab, not GitHub — 595 stars, last activity 2026-08-12; @antora/cli 3.1.15 published 2026-05-26.

tools.name: Sphinx
tools.one_line: Twenty years old and still the only one here that ships both a machine-readable cross-reference inventory (objects.inv) and a link checker that writes output.json and sets exit status 1.
tools.notable: `objects.inv` is the sleeper feature: every HTML build emits a compressed inventory mapping every documented object name to a URI relative to the doc root, keyed by domain and object type (py:class, std:doc, std:label, …), and it is directly inspectable — `python -m sphinx.ext.intersphinx https://docs.python.org/3/objects.inv` dumps all links and targets. That is a published, typed, cross-project resolution artifact: any other project can resolve links into yours without a server. The linkcheck builder is a real gate, verified in source (sphinx/builders/linkcheck.py): it writes both `output.txt` and `output.json` into outdir and sets `self._app.statuscode = 1` on breakage. Reference integrity for internal targets: `-n / --nitpicky` warns on all missing references, with `nitpick_ignore` / `nitpick_ignore_regex` providing a *pinned, individually-listed* exemption set of (warning_type, target) tuples; `-W / --fail-on-warning` turns warnings into exit status 1, and since Sphinx 8.1 it runs the whole build first rather than bailing on the first warning (--keep-going always on). Machine-readable builders: json (.fjson fragments plus globalcontext.json and searchindex.json), xml (Docutils-native), pickle, pseudoxml. Provenance is first-class through autodoc/viewcode/linkcode, which tie rendered docs back to the defining source. Typed cross-references via domains are validated; document-level content types are not. Latest 9.1.0; GitHub reports NOASSERTION but LICENSE.rst states two-clause BSD 'unless otherwise indicated'.

tools.name: Astro Starlight
tools.one_line: The strongest typed-frontmatter story in the set — extensible Zod schemas that fail the build and emit JSON Schema — paired with the weakest first-party gate and agent story, both of which are community plugins.
tools.notable: Frontmatter is validated by Zod through Astro content collections: `docsSchema()` in src/content.config.ts defines the docs collection, and its `extend` option takes a Zod schema so teams add their own required typed fields — the closest thing in this landscape to a user-definable content-type system. Astro fails the build when a file violates its collection schema, and generates JSON Schema per collection into `.astro/collections/<name>.schema.json` plus inferred TypeScript interfaces — i.e. it publishes a machine-readable description of your own doc types, which is precisely the artifact a closed typed-concept system should be emitting. What it does not have first-party: link validation (community HiDeoo/starlight-links-validator, MIT, 120 stars, pushed 2026-08-12, which also invalidates the content-layer cache so links revalidate; note a documented Astro v5 regression where pages with custom IDs/slugs can no longer be validated and get flagged invalid), llms.txt (community delucis/starlight-llms-txt, MIT, 108 stars, pushed 2026-08-02), and AI surfaces (community starlight-biel chatbot, starlight-agentready). The plugins page lists exactly one official plugin — Algolia DocSearch, replacing the default Pagefind provider. Default search is Pagefind full-text keyword, local and offline, not semantic. Provenance is editLink/lastUpdated only. @astrojs/starlight 0.41.7 published 2026-08-05.

tools.name: Mintlify
tools.one_line: Has repositioned entirely around agents — auto-hosted MCP, auto-generated skill.md, llms.txt, and a `mint score` agent-readiness grader — but it is a hosted proprietary platform and the CLI is Elastic-2.0, not open source.
tools.notable: CLI surface (`mint`, npm, Elastic-2.0, 4.2.799 published 2026-08-12): dev, broken-links, a11y, validate, score, deslop, format, config, index, plus signup/login/new. Two are without parallel elsewhere: `mint score` grades agent-navigation readiness against 29 checks and accepts an arbitrary URL, so you can score a competitor's docs; `mint deslop` flags AI-generated prose and suggests human-style revisions. `mint validate` runs the build in strict mode and exits with an error on any warning or error; `mint format` exits 1 with the offending file path, explicitly for CI. MCP is auto-generated and cloud-hosted at /mcp (or /authed/mcp), exposing three tools — search over indexed content, a 'query docs filesystem' tool browsing a virtual filesystem with shell-style commands, and submit-feedback — and it surfaces skill.md files as MCP *resources*. skill.md is auto-regenerated on every docs update, consolidating capabilities, limitations and best practices that documentation normally scatters, and installs into 20+ coding agents. llms.txt and llms-full.txt are automatic at both /llms.txt and /.well-known/llms.txt, advertised via `Link: </llms.txt>; rel="llms-txt"` and `X-Llms-Txt` response headers, hard-capped at 100,000 characters with truncation beyond, and every entry links a `.md` URL. docs.json is JSON-Schema-validated against https://mintlify.com/docs.json. Caveats that matter: the broken-link CI check is NOT on by default — you enable it on the dashboard at Warning (never blocks) or Blocking level, and CI checks require Pro/Enterprise; the assistant, agent, contextual menu and MCP all require explicit enablement, while markdown serving, llms.txt/skill.md hosting and semantic search are automatic.

tools.name: Fern
tools.one_line: The most CLI-shaped competitor: `fern check` is a real local validation gate, `fern docs link check --output json` emits machine-readable link results, and `fern diff` returns a JSON verdict with a semantic exit code.
tools.notable: `fern check` validates the API definition and Fern configuration — fern.config.json, generators.yml, docs.yml — and its rule set includes a `broken-links` rule that resolves internal links against the LOCAL navigation tree rather than crawling a live site, i.e. a deterministic offline link gate; flags are --api and --warnings. Complementary commands: `fern docs md check` validates MDX syntax across every page referenced in navigation; `fern docs link check --url --output text|json|csv` crawls the published site for internal and external breakage; `fern docs diff --output <dir>` produces visual side-by-side screenshot diffs of preview vs production, built for GitHub Actions. The pattern worth stealing is `fern diff --from-version`: it prints a JSON object containing the computed semver bump and the next version, and exits non-zero when the bump is major — a machine-readable verdict wired to a meaningful exit code, which is exactly lore's impact-command shape. AI surface is explicitly split automatic vs opt-in: MCP server (auto-generated and hosted at /_mcp/server for any site with Ask Fern, disableable via `mcp: false` in page-actions, FERN_TOKEN header on authenticated sites), llms.txt (automatic, with the notable refinement that appending /llms.txt to ANY page URL yields a page-scoped index, and .md yields that page's markdown), markdown .md endpoints (automatic, framed as token reduction), API catalog discovery (automatic); opt-in and credit-metered are Ask Fern (2 credits/message), Fern Writer (a Slack agent that opens docs PRs, 50 credits/session), AI-generated examples (1 credit each) and Agent Skills (a pre-built `fern-docs` skill plus custom skill hosting). CLI is Apache-2.0 open source (fern-api/fern, 3753 stars, pushed 2026-08-13; fern-api 5.95.0 published 2026-08-12); the docs platform and every AI feature are hosted SaaS on a credit plan.

tools.name: AGENTS.md
tools.one_line: Convention (not a schema): a plain-Markdown "README for agents" at repo root, contributed by OpenAI and now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation; the site repo agentsmd/agents.md is just the Next.js website and has been quiet since 2026-03-12, but the format itself is the broadest cross-tool convergence point in this category.
tools.notable: Cross-tool reach is the whole feature. Linux Foundation press release (2025-12-09) and agents.md both state "more than 60,000 open source projects". agents.md names 23+ reading tools: Codex, Jules, Factory, Aider, goose, opencode, Zed, Warp, VS Code, Devin, UiPath, Junie, Amp, Cursor, RooCode, Gemini CLI, Kilo Code, Phoenix, Semgrep, GitHub Copilot Coding Agent, Ona, Windsurf, Augment Code. Codex implements a precise, documented resolution algorithm a docs CLI can target: per-directory order AGENTS.override.md -> AGENTS.md -> project_doc_fallback_filenames (defaults include TEAM_GUIDE.md, .agents.md); global ~/.codex/AGENTS.md first, then root-to-leaf concatenation joined by blank lines, capped by project_doc_max_bytes = 32 KiB by default with files silently skipped past the cap. Cursor supports nested AGENTS.md in any subdirectory with closest-file-wins. GitHub Copilot reads AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and GEMINI.md as "agent instructions", below .github/copilot-instructions.md in precedence. What it lacks: the canonical repo contains no schema, no JSON Schema, no linter, and no validator (full tree enumerated: AGENTS.md, README.md, LICENSE, and Next.js website source only), and the site states "no required fields" and "AGENTS.md is just standard Markdown. Use any headings you like."

tools.name: Agent Skills (SKILL.md) — agentskills.io
tools.one_line: Open spec for a skill folder (SKILL.md + optional scripts/, references/, assets/) with genuinely constrained frontmatter and a reference validator; originally Anthropic, released as an open standard, adopted by ~45 named clients including Cursor, Codex/ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, VS Code, Gemini CLI, opencode, goose, Amp, Factory, Junie, Roo Code, Kiro and Claude Code.
tools.notable: The only surface in this category with a real, enforceable schema and a validator command. Spec constraints: name 1-64 chars, unicode lowercase a-z/0-9/hyphen only, no leading/trailing hyphen, no consecutive hyphens, and must match the parent directory name; description 1-1024 chars non-empty; compatibility 1-500 chars; metadata is a string->string map; allowed-tools a space-separated string (marked Experimental). Exactly six fields — anything else is out of spec, and Claude Code's spec-path validators emit "Unexpected key(s) in SKILL.md frontmatter... Allowed properties are: allowed-tools, compatibility, description, license, metadata, name". Reference CLI `skills-ref` (agentskills/agentskills/skills-ref, Python, self-described "for demonstration purposes only") offers `skills-ref validate <dir>`, `skills-ref read-properties <dir>` (outputs JSON), and `skills-ref to-prompt <dir>...` which emits an `<available_skills>` XML block for agent prompts. Token budgeting is specified numerically, not hand-waved: metadata ~100 tokens loaded at startup for every skill, SKILL.md body <5000 tokens recommended and <500 lines, resources loaded only on demand. Path portability matters for a generator: Cursor loads skills from `.agents/skills/`, `.cursor/skills/`, `~/.agents/skills/`, `~/.cursor/skills/`, and "For compatibility, Cursor also loads skills from Claude and Codex directories: `.claude/skills/`, `.codex/skills/`, `~/.claude/skills/`, and `~/.codex/skills/`."

tools.name: CLAUDE.md + .claude/rules/ (Claude Code memory)
tools.one_line: Anthropic-proprietary, actively developed instruction surface (docs reference Claude Code v2.1.227 as of 2026-08-12): hierarchical CLAUDE.md files loaded root-to-leaf, plus path-scoped `.claude/rules/*.md`; critically, Claude Code does NOT read AGENTS.md.
tools.notable: The decisive finding for a SKILL.md-bridge generator, quoted verbatim: "Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md`, not `AGENTS.md`. If your repository already uses `AGENTS.md` for other coding agents, create a `CLAUDE.md` that imports it so both tools read the same instructions without duplicating them." The documented bridge is a CLAUDE.md whose first line is `@AGENTS.md` followed by Claude-specific content, or `ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md` when no Claude-specific content is needed (symlink needs Administrator or Developer Mode on Windows, so the import is the portable form). Other machinery a repo-resident docs CLI can hook: `@path/to/import` expansion with max depth 4 hops, import parsing skipping code spans/fences, an approval dialog for imports resolving outside the working dir; `.claude/rules/*.md` with YAML `paths:` glob frontmatter (bounded at 1,000 expanded patterns / 4 MiB per rule) so instructions load only when Claude touches matching files; `claudeMdExcludes` glob list merged across settings layers; managed-policy CLAUDE.md and a `claudeMd` key in managed-settings.json; block-level HTML comments stripped before injection so maintainer notes cost no tokens; the `InstructionsLoaded` hook to log exactly which instruction files loaded and why. Auto memory is separate and LLM-written: `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/MEMORY.md`, hard-capped at the first 200 lines or 25KB with an over-limit write error, and a `modified` ISO 8601 frontmatter timestamp recorded on write. `/init` with CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT=1 reads AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules/, .cursorrules, .github/copilot-instructions.md, .devin/rules/, .windsurf/rules/, .windsurfrules, .clinerules; `/import` (v2.1.213+) appends a one-time copy of AGENTS.md into CLAUDE.md.

tools.name: Cursor Rules (.cursor/rules/*.mdc, legacy .cursorrules)
tools.one_line: Proprietary, vendor-specific rule format in `.cursor/rules/` as `.mdc` files with description/globs/alwaysApply frontmatter; the root `.cursorrules` file is legacy — the string "cursorrules" no longer appears anywhere on the current rules docs page (verified by full-text scan of the fetched page on 2026-08-12).
tools.notable: Four documented activation modes a docs generator can target deliberately: Always Apply (ignores globs/description), Apply Intelligently (model picks from `description`), Apply to Specific Files (glob auto-attach), Apply Manually (`@rule-name`). Precedence is Team Rules -> Project Rules -> User Rules. Notably, plain `.md` files in `.cursor/rules/` are ignored — with one exception: `AGENTS.md`. Cursor supports nested AGENTS.md: "You can place `AGENTS.md` files in any subdirectory of your project, and they will be automatically applied when working with files in that directory or its children," with more specific instructions taking precedence. Cursor separately loads SKILL.md skills and, for compatibility, reads `.claude/skills/` and `.codex/skills/` — so an existing Claude Code SKILL.md bridge already reaches Cursor without any Cursor-specific emission. No rules validator, JSON output, or CI gate found in the docs (marked unknown, not checked exhaustively).

tools.name: llms.txt (v2)
tools.one_line: Jeremy Howard's informal community proposal (v1 2024-09-03, v2 published 2026-08-10) for a curated Markdown index served at /llms.txt or any subpath, plus .md mirrors of HTML pages; a convention with a precise grammar and a reference Python parser, not a standards-body spec and not a service.
tools.notable: Explicitly designed for deterministic machine parsing — "llms.txt markdown is human and LLM readable, but is also in a precise format allowing fixed processing methods (i.e. classical programming techniques such as parsers and regex)." Fixed section order: optional BOM; H1 project name (the only required section); blockquote summary; zero or more non-heading markdown sections; zero or more H2-delimited "file lists" whose items are `[name](url)` optionally followed by `: notes`. The `## Optional` H2 is a load-bearing convention: "links an agent can skip when a shorter context is needed" — a two-tier context budget expressed in the document itself. Reference implementation `llms-txt` on PyPI (v0.0.6, Apache-2.0) ships two console scripts, `llms_txt2ctx` and `llms_txt2html`, over a regex parser (`llms_txt/core.py`: `parse_link`, `parse_llms_file`, `mk_ctx`, `get_sizes`, `create_ctx`; plus `llms_txt/miniparse.py` and `tests/test-parse.py`). v2 adds discovery link relations a docs site can emit as HTML `<link>` or an HTTP header: `Link: </docs/page.html.md>; rel="alternate"; type="text/markdown", </docs/llms.txt>; rel="describedby"`, plus most-specific-path-wins resolution when several llms.txt files apply. Adoption is real and named on the spec page: thousands of sites, Chrome Lighthouse audits for it under agentic-browsing checks, and OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini all publish one for their developer docs; generators exist in Mintlify, GitBook, Yoast SEO, AIOSEO, Wix, vitepress-plugin-llms, docusaurus-plugin-llms, llms-txt-php, Drupal. No link checker, no graph, no MCP server (full repo tree enumerated).

tools.name: Context7
tools.one_line: Upstash's hosted documentation-retrieval platform (MIT client, proprietary cloud service): an MCP server, a `ctx7` CLI, and SDKs that fetch version-specific library docs; free tier is public libraries at 1,000 API calls/month, and private repos require Pro ($10/seat/mo) or Enterprise with content parsed into Context7's cloud.
tools.notable: Two MCP tools only: `resolve-library-id` (params `query`, `libraryName`) and `query-docs` (params `libraryId` e.g. `/vercel/next.js`, `query`). CLI mirrors them: `ctx7 library <name> <query>` and `ctx7 docs <libraryId> <query>`. Setup installs an Agent Skill that "guides your agent to fetch docs using `ctx7` CLI commands" — i.e. it ships a static skill rather than generating one from your content. Relevance-ranked natural-language retrieval is the core capability a deterministic repo-resident CLI does not have. Private-source ingestion spans GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, other Git providers, Confluence, and OpenAPI specs, with role-gated (Owners/Admins) management, incremental refresh billed only on changed content, and an "only accepting GitHub repos with more than 1,000 stars"-style trust policy filter at Enterprise. Answers the brief's upload question directly: yes for private content, and self-hosted deployment is Enterprise-only. Published pricing: Free $0 / 1,000 calls per month / no private repos; Pro $10 per seat per month / 5,000 calls per seat / $10 per additional 1,000 calls / private repos included; private parsing billed at $25 per 1M tokens; Enterprise custom, $30/user/mo for small teamspaces down to $2.50/user/mo at volume, adding SOC-2, SAML/OIDC SSO, and self-hosting.

tools.name: DeepWiki / Devin Wiki (Cognition)
tools.one_line: Cognition's LLM-generated repository wiki — architecture diagrams, page hierarchies, source links, and conversational Q&A; free and unauthenticated for public GitHub repos at deepwiki.com plus a free public MCP server, with private repos requiring the Devin app and repository indexing on Cognition's infrastructure. "Devin Wiki" is the same product surfaced in the Devin app sidebar, not a separate one.
tools.notable: Free public MCP server at `https://mcp.deepwiki.com/mcp` (streamable HTTP; `/sse` deprecated), documented as "a free, remote, no-authentication-required service that provides access to public repositories", exposing exactly three tools whose shape is instructive: `read_wiki_structure` (list documentation topics for a repo), `read_wiki_contents` (view the documentation), `ask_question` (context-grounded Q&A). Private repos use `https://mcp.devin.ai/mcp` with a bearer token. Install line: `claude mcp add -s user -t http deepwiki https://mcp.deepwiki.com/mcp`. The repo-resident steering file is the most directly transferable idea: `.devin/wiki.json` at repo root, with a `repo_notes` array (max 10,000 characters per note, max 100 notes total) and a `pages` array of explicit titles/purposes with optional parent relationships (max 30 pages, titles must be unique and non-empty) — and "If `pages` is provided, we'll bypass the default cluster-based planning and create exactly the pages you specify." Also ships a JSON REST API for indexing lifecycle (v2 get repository indexing status; v3 list indexed repositories, bulk index repositories) and per-branch indexing.
