Generated wikis include "links to sources", giving claim-to-code provenance, but the whole artifact is LLM-generated and therefore non-reproducible.

tools.name: npryce/adr-tools
tools.one_line: The de-facto standard bash ADR scripts, but effectively unmaintained: the last commit on master (its only branch) is 2020-03-30, over six years stale, despite a 2024-04-25 pushed_at on the GitHub API.
tools.notable: `adr link SOURCE LINK TARGET REVERSE-LINK` writes BOTH directions of a relation in a single call (forward link into the source, reverse link into the target) - reciprocal-link authoring as a CLI primitive rather than a validation afterthought. `adr generate graph [-p PREFIX] [-e EXT]` emits Graphviz DOT with a dotted chronological spine (_n-1 -> _n) plus labelled relation edges, filtering out the ' by' reverse edges so the graph is not doubled. `adr generate` with no argument self-discovers report types by globbing `src/_adr_generate_*`, so adding a report is a file drop. GPL-3.0, which matters if anything were ever vendored. Cells above are checked against a full enumeration of `src/` (the complete command surface), not inferred: there is no validate, check, JSON, or task command.

tools.name: thomvaill/log4brains
tools.one_line: ADR knowledge-base generator that publishes a static site; stale - last commit and last npm release (v1.1.0) are both 2024-12-17, roughly 20 months before the 2026-08-12 observation date.
tools.notable: Relations are DERIVED FROM ORDINARY MARKDOWN LINKS rather than declared in frontmatter: the domain has a first-class `AdrRelation(from, relation, to)` plus `MarkdownAdrLink`, resolved by an injectable `MarkdownAdrLinkResolver` interface. Authors write prose links and get a typed graph, which is a materially different authoring ergonomic from a `relatesTo:` field. Deliberately imposes no file-numbering scheme, to avoid git merge conflicts on ADR numbers. Derives ADR author and dates from git log, so CI must checkout with `fetch-depth: 0`. Two gaps verified in source rather than assumed: the full CLI is only `adr new` and `adr list` (`--raw`, tab-style, not JSON) plus global `init`/`preview`/`build`, and the link resolver returns `undefined` for an unresolvable ADR link with no warning, so broken links are silently dropped from the relation graph rather than reported. The `@adr` annotation for code references is listed in the README under 'Coming soon' and never shipped.

tools.name: adr/madr (Markdown Architectural Decision Records)
tools.one_line: A template specification, not a tool - the npm package declares `"files": ["template/"]` and ships no bin, so it standardizes how a decision is written and enforces nothing about it afterward; repo is maintained (commits through 2026-07-07) but the last release is 4.0.0 from 2024-09-17.
tools.notable: MADR 4 frontmatter carries `status`, `date`, `decision-makers`, `consulted`, `informed` - but the template's own first comment reads 'These are optional metadata elements. Feel free to remove any of them.', and supersession is encoded as free text inside the status string (`superseded by ADR-0123`) rather than as a typed reference. That is precisely why a downstream tool has to define a strict superset before anything can be machine-checked. Ships four granularity tiers (full / minimal / bare / bare-minimal) plus i18n variants, and is dual-licensed MIT OR CC0-1.0 so templates can be vendored with no attribution burden. The lychee link-check and markdownlint workflows in `.github/workflows/` gate MADR's OWN repository; they are not shipped to consumers, so a MADR adopter inherits no gate.

tools.name: mbeacom/adrkit
tools.one_line: Machine-readable ADRs with a strict MADR-superset schema, a CI gate, a model-free evaluator and a read-only MCP server - architecturally the closest analogue to lore in this whole landscape, but brand new (repo created 2026-07-18, v0.7.0, 6 stars) and self-declared as having 'no external adopters or production users yet'.
tools.notable: Five things a repo-resident docs CLI typically lacks. (1) DOCS-TO-CODE COUPLING IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: each record declares `affects` matchers (path globs, package ranges) and any source file can opt in with an `@adr 0012` comment marker in any language with no schema change; `adr explain <path>` prints every governing decision AND why it governs, keeping the two routes distinct (`via path: src/**` vs `declared by src/sync.ts:3`). (2) CORPUS FINGERPRINT AS A FIRST-CLASS RESPONSE FIELD: every MCP response carries `corpusHealth { fingerprint, recordCount, excludedCount }`, and pagination cursors are bound to that fingerprint plus the query shape, so a stale cursor returns a typed non-error `invalid-cursor` outcome (`corpus-changed`, `query-mismatch`, `wrong-channel`, `offset-out-of-range`, `cursor-not-applicable`, `version-unsupported`, `decode-failed`) instead of silently wrong data. (3) FEDERATED CROSS-REPO REFS WITH INERT-ON-ABSENT SEMANTICS: a `<log>:<id>` ref resolves against a supplied federated-log snapshot; if that log has no snapshot the ref is `federated-log-absent` and INERT, never a dangling-link failure (`packages/evaluator/src/rules/no-orphan-refs.ts`). (4) OVERSIZE HANDLING BY EXCLUSION, NOT TRUNCATION: 64 KiB per-record cap, oversized records excluded and surfaced as a `record-too-large` finding. (5) A model-free `adr evaluate <proposal> --snapshot <bundle.json> --date YYYY-MM-DD` Pass 0 that routes to a named human and explicitly 'never approves, persists, or writes'. Limits: graph is a build-and-render (`buildAdrGraph` -> nodes/edges/DOT), and the MCP README names 'no transitive supersession traversal' as an explicit boundary; exit codes are effectively 0/1 from `exitCodeForFindings` plus 2 for a malformed bundle, not a wide taxonomy. `adr queue` couples to an ARB review workflow (tiers, SLA, approvals, objections) rather than a general task tracker. Published as `@adrkit/cli` and `@adrkit/mcp` v0.7.0 (Apache-2.0, 2026-08-12); MCP registry id `dev.adrkit/mcp`.

tools.name: adr/ad-guidance-tool (adg)
tools.one_line: Go CLI from the ADR org that compiles decisions into EXECUTABLE architecture rules verified against the filesystem, with an MCP server built for agent rule-authoring; small and young (created 2025-06-23, v1.1.0 on 2026-06-25).
tools.notable: The decision -> `.rule` -> enforcement chain makes an ADR executable, which no markdown docs CLI does: `adg enforce rule --model M --id N` generates a rule template from an existing decision, `adg enforce compile` turns rules into architecture tests (Go, .NET) via plugins, and `adg enforce verify` checks rules directly against the filesystem - all delegated to ADE (ad-enforcement-tool) through a plugin system with `adg enforce plugin` for install/update. The MCP server is shaped as a generate-then-validate loop for the agent rather than a retrieval endpoint: `list_adrs`, `get_adr` (returns the content AND the path where its rule file should go), `get_dsl_reference` (serves the whole rule-DSL grammar on demand), `list_rule_files` (in-repo examples as few-shot material), `validate_rule` (parses candidate rule text with the real ADE parser before the agent commits it). Also has `adg merge` and `adg import` for combining decision models across projects, `adg copy --model ... --target` for subsetting a model by filter, and `adg revise` which clones a decision and resets it to 'open'. Caveat found in source: `ModelValidateInteractor.Validate` carries `// TODO: also validate that decision metadata is correct (all required fields are available)`, so schema validation is index-and-data consistency only today. No `--json` output mode found in the README or command list.

tools.name: SCIP (scip-code/scip)
tools.one_line: Actively maintained Protobuf code-index format that has been TRANSFERRED OUT OF SOURCEGRAPH to the vendor-neutral `scip-code` org - `api.github.com/repos/sourcegraph/scip` now returns a 301 to the new repo, so an existence check on the brief's URL still returns 200 through the redirect and would confirm a stale citation.
tools.notable: SCIP EXPLICITLY REFUSES to be the thing a graph/impact CLI needs, which is the most useful finding here for scoping a join. DESIGN.md: SCIP 'is meant to be a _transmission_ format ... it is not meant as a _storage_ format for querying'; 'Support efficient code navigation by itself' is listed under NON-GOALS with the rationale that bidirectional lookup 'is best served by a query engine'; and 'Avoid direct encoding of graphs' is a named core design decision. So there is no query language and no depends-on answer - the consumer builds that. The sanctioned escape hatch is `scip expt-convert`, which converts an index into a SQLite database ('For inspecting the data, use the SQLite CLI. For inspecting the schema, use .schema'), with occurrences stored as an opaque blob to stop the DB exploding. Full CLI is `lint`, `print --json`, `snapshot`, `stats`, `test`, `expt-convert`. Note a name collision worth avoiding: `scip snapshot` generates GOLDEN-TEST files for indexer output, not a temporal snapshot of a corpus. Incrementality is a stated design goal ('Adding file-level incrementality should be easy') delegated to indexers, not a feature of the format's tooling. Ten indexers listed, most still under `sourcegraph/*`.

tools.name: LSIF (microsoft/lsif-node)
tools.one_line: The predecessor graph format to SCIP and the one that DOES encode an explicit graph (vertices + edges as newline-delimited JSON); the repo still receives dependency bumps but its README still calls the spec 'a first draft' and the tools 'work in progress', and Sourcegraph has 'fully deprecated and removed' LSIF support.
tools.notable: MONIKERS are the feature worth stealing and the one thing in this set that solves 'join two independently-produced graphs'. A language-internal symbol id is meaningless across repos, so LSIF defines monikers as stable cross-package identifiers and ships a conversion step: `lsif tsc -p tsconfig.json --package package.json --stdout` bakes npm monikers in, or you pipe `lsif tsc --stdout | lsif npm --stdin --package package.json --stdout` to inspect the newly generated ones separately. That two-stage local-id-then-ecosystem-id design is exactly the shape a docs graph needs to reference a code graph without either side owning the other's namespace. The dump is JSON Lines, so it streams. Note that LSIF's integer-id, directly-encoded-graph design is what SCIP later rejected by name ('Avoiding integer IDs', 'Avoid direct encoding of graphs'), so treat LSIF as a cautionary reference rather than a target. Most 2026 commits are dependabot; last substantive commit 2026-05-11 (replace UUID with crypto for ID generation). Cells marked unknown were not checked - only the README and the format were read.

tools.name: Meta Glean
tools.one_line: Meta's fact database for source code, with a real Datalog-derived query language (Angle), genuinely incremental stacked databases and a CLI plus Thrift server - by far the strongest query ergonomics in this set and by far the heaviest to operate (Haskell, RocksDB).
tools.notable: Sets the query bar. `glean query --db NAME/INSTANCE "QUERY"` executes Angle from the CLI (`@file` or `-` for stdin, `--limit FACTS`, `--stats FILE`, `-o FILE`); `glean list --format (tty|plain|json|compact-json)` is explicitly documented as 'useful for processing and filtering the result in a script, e.g. using jq'. `glean validate` and `glean validate-schema` are separate subcommands, so schema conformance is a distinct verb from data conformance. DERIVED PREDICATES are the standout idea: you define a rule once and `glean derive` MATERIALIZES the derived facts into the database, which is how an expensive traversal gets precomputed rather than re-walked per query. INCREMENTALITY works by STACKING databases - an increment is a DB stacked on the base that hides units and propagates new ownership, increments can stack on other increments, and incremental derivation is intended to cost time proportional to the size of the increment. Databases are addressed `NAME/INSTANCE`, so every query pins an exact instance, which is snapshot addressing for free. Two real limits: Angle 'currently supports non-recursive queries only', so unbounded transitive closure (true blast radius) is not directly expressible and must be staged through derived predicates; and there is no MCP server (verified by repo code search for `modelcontextprotocol` returning zero, and by the CLI subcommand list: create, write, finish, dump, delete, derive, index, query, restore, validate, validate-schema, stats, unfinish, list). GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION; the LICENSE file is a Facebook BSD License.

tools.name: GitHub Stack Graphs
tools.one_line: ARCHIVED AND ABANDONED - GitHub archived the repo on 2025-09-09 and the README opens with 'This repository is no longer supported or updated by GitHub. If you wish to continue to develop this code yourself, we recommend you fork it.'
tools.notable: The idea worth preserving even though the code is dead: INCREMENTALITY WITHOUT A BUILD SYSTEM. Stack graphs are built per-file from a tree-sitter parse plus declarative TSG name-resolution rules, and the README states they are 'efficient, incremental, and do[] not need to tap into existing build or program analysis tools' - so a file's graph fragment is computable in isolation and name resolution happens later by path-finding across fragments. The CLI workflow is `tree-sitter-stack-graphs index SOURCE_DIR` (which 'will skip any files that have already be indexed', `-f` to force), `status SOURCE_DIR`, `clean [--delete]`, and `query definition SOURCE_PATH:LINE:COLUMN`. Note the CLI exposes DEFINITION LOOKUP ONLY - no find-references verb, so no blast-radius answer from the command line even though the underlying model is bidirectional. `tree-sitter-stack-graphs init PROJECT_DIR` interactively scaffolds a whole new language project. Based on Eelco Visser's scope graphs work at TU Delft. Cells marked unknown reflect that only the documented workflow was read, not the full `-h` surface.

tools.name: ast-grep
tools.one_line: Very actively maintained Rust structural search, lint and rewrite tool with excellent CI-gate and JSON ergonomics - but no cross-file graph of any kind; its relational rules traverse the AST within a single file.
tools.notable: Best-in-class JSON and gate ergonomics: `--json=pretty|stream|compact` (stream is JSON Lines, one object per match), exit 1 when any error-severity rule matches and 0 otherwise, and per-rule severity OVERRIDE FLAGS at invocation time - `--error[=<RULE_ID>...]`, `--warning[=...]`, `--info`, `--hint`, `--off` - so one rule set serves both an advisory local run and a blocking CI run without editing the rules. The MCP server (ast-grep/ast-grep-mcp, MIT, 447 stars, pushed 2026-08-12) is built as a GENERATE -> TEST -> RUN loop rather than a search endpoint: `dump_syntax_tree(code, language, format=cst|ast|pattern)` lets the agent inspect how ast-grep parses both the target code AND its own candidate pattern, `test_match_code_rule(code, yaml)` validates a rule against a snippet before it ever touches the repo, then `find_code` / `find_code_by_rule` run it. It even raises a teaching error on no-match ('Try adding `stopBy: end` to your inside/has rule'). It ships `ast-grep.mdc`, a Cursor rules file that scripts that exact five-step loop, and an LLM-oriented text formatter that collapses JSON matches to `file:start-end` plus match text with a `max_results` cap. Verified absent from the CLI reference (run, outline, scan, test, new, lsp, completions): any dependency graph, call graph or find-references. `ast-grep test` uses golden snapshots for RULE testing, which is not corpus-state diffing.

tools.name: Sourcebot
tools.one_line: Self-hosted code search and agent context layer, extremely actively developed, but licensed FSL-1.1-ALv2 (source-available, not OSI open source, converts to Apache-2.0 later) with an additional proprietary `ee/` tree - and the MCP server sits in `ee/` behind a license key.
tools.notable: THE MOST RIGOROUSLY TOKEN-BUDGETED MCP SURFACE IN THIS SET - every tool documents a hard cap and its truncation behaviour, which is a discipline a docs MCP should copy wholesale: `read_file` takes `offset` plus `limit` with a max of 500 lines; `list_tree` takes `depth` (1-10, default 1) and `maxEntries` (1-10000, default 1000) and states it truncates; `grep` and `glob` default `limit` 100; `list_repos` and `list_commits` are `page`/`perPage` paginated with perPage max 100. Second idea worth stealing: EVERY read tool accepts a `ref` (commit SHA, branch or tag), so an agent can pin an entire investigation to one commit, and `get_diff(repo, base, head)` diffs two refs directly. Eleven tools total: grep, list_repos, read_file, list_tree, list_commits, glob, get_diff, find_symbol_definitions, find_symbol_references, list_language_models, ask_codebase. `find_symbol_references` is the one-hop depends-on answer. `ask_codebase` is explicitly LLM-backed - it 'uses Sourcebot's existing code search and navigation tools to allow reasoning models to search your code' and returns answers 'rich with inline citations and navigable code snippets', i.e. agentic retrieval over deterministic primitives rather than embedding search. Transport is Streamable HTTP at `/api/mcp` with OAuth 2.0 (paid) or `Authorization: Bearer <API key>`. There is a real custom search query language with a Lezer grammar in `packages/queryLanguage`, but it is a search DSL, not graph traversal. It is a deployed server with a database, not a CLI, so there is no exit-code contract.

tools.name: Nx project graph
tools.one_line: Monorepo build system whose project graph gives the cleanest blast-radius answer in this landscape: `nx show projects --affected --json` computes the transitive impact of a git range and prints it as JSON.
tools.notable: The impact query is the reference implementation. `nx show projects --affected` accepts `--base`, `--head`, `--untracked`, `--uncommitted`, `--files`, and the yargs config wires each of those with `.implies(..., 'affected')` so none of them can be passed WITHOUT `--affected` - the CLI makes the incoherent invocation unrepresentable rather than validating it after the fact. It also declares `.conflicts('sep','json')` in both directions so the output-format choice is exclusive. `NX_BASE` / `NX_HEAD` env vars mirror the flags for CI. The graph itself is a plain typed JSON document, verified in source: `interface ProjectGraph { nodes: Record<string, ProjectGraphProjectNode>; externalNodes?: ...; dependencies: Record<string, ProjectGraphDependency[]>; version?: string }`, dumped by `nx graph --file=output.json`, with `DependencyType` distinguishing `static` (a real import) from `dynamic` and `implicit` (a declared dependency) - an edge-kind distinction a docs graph needs too, to separate 'this doc links that doc' from 'this doc is declared to govern that task'. `nx graph --focus <project>` scopes the view. MCP server is `nx-mcp` on npm (v0.25.0, MIT, from nrwl/nx-console, last published 2026-06-04) exposing `nx_workspace`, `nx_workspace_path`, `nx_project_details`, `nx_visualize_graph`, `nx_docs`, `nx_generators`, `nx_generator_schema`, `nx_available_plugins`, `ci_information`, `ci_task_output`, `nx_current_running_tasks_details`, `nx_current_running_task_output`.

tools.name: CodeQL
tools.one_line: The most powerful query language here (QL, a statically-typed object-oriented Datalog with dataflow libraries) and the only tool in this set with a fully documented exit-code taxonomy - but databases are built by full extraction rather than incrementally, and the CLI binaries are not MIT (github/codeql-cli-binaries reports NOASSERTION; only the queries and libraries in github/codeql are MIT).
tools.notable: THE EXIT-CODE TAXONOMY IS THE SINGLE BEST ARTIFACT TO COPY: 0 success; 1 'the command successfully determined that the answer to your question is no' (used by test run, dataset check, query format, resolve extractor); 2 something went wrong, human-readable message on stderr; 3 launcher could not find the CodeQL installation directory; 32 THE EXTRACTOR DIDN'T FIND ANY CODE TO ANALYZE; 33 one or more query evaluations timed out; 98 evaluation explicitly cancelled; 99 out of memory; 100 fatal internal error. Note what 1 and 32 buy: a clean semantic 'no' that is distinct from an error, and NON-VACUITY AS ITS OWN FAILURE CODE, so an empty or mis-scoped run can never be mistaken for a clean pass. Query kinds matter too: `@kind path-problem` returns the ENTIRE path from source to sink rather than just the endpoint, and `@kind graph` queries render via `--format=dot|dgml|graphtext` alongside the normal `--format=sarif-latest|sarifv2.1.0|csv`. There is no `--format=json` - SARIF is the JSON. Databases are point-in-time: the docs give no guidance on updating an existing database when code changes, and for C# recommend adding `/t:rebuild` or a prior `dotnet clean` 'to ensure that all code will be built', so re-creation is the model. MCP is adjacent rather than built in: `advanced-security/codeql-development-mcp-server` (GitHub CodeQL Expert Services team per CODEOWNERS, 31 stars, pushed 2026-08-12) wraps query compilation, execution, testing and database operations, but ships with 'no expectation or guarantee of support'.

adoption_candidates.feature: SARIF 2.1.0 output from the validator, with an --exit-zero variant so the upload step always runs
adoption_candidates.seen_in: okfcli/okf (`okf validate --format sarif --exit-zero`), open-doc-spec/ods (`ods lint --format sarif`)
adoption_candidates.why: Turns `lore check` findings into native GitHub PR annotations and Security-tab entries with no glue code. Two independent implementations converged on it and it is strictly additive to lore's existing exit codes. The --exit-zero variant matters: a failing gate otherwise skips the upload step and you lose the annotations exactly when you need them.

adoption_candidates.feature: Stable per-finding rule IDs (okf/links/broken, okf/frontmatter/type-required) instead of message text
adoption_candidates.why: lore already has stable exit codes; rule IDs are the same discipline one level down. They let CI and agents suppress, route or ratchet an individual check without regex-matching prose, and they make a message-wording change a non-breaking edit. They also pair directly with SARIF, which wants a ruleId per result.

adoption_candidates.feature: A `schema` command that emits the CLI's own complete machine-readable surface (commands, flags, args, output shape, exit codes) as JSON
adoption_candidates.why: An agent driving lore currently has to read `lore instructions` prose. One `lore schema` call would let any agent — not just one primed by the .claude/skills/lore skill — discover the whole verb surface and the exit-code contract deterministically. Cheapest available improvement to lore's agent-drivability, and it composes with the JSON envelopes lore already emits.

adoption_candidates.feature: `--max-warnings N` as a ratchet alongside `--strict`
adoption_candidates.why: OKF §11 forbids rejecting a bundle for broken links, so a conformant validator cannot hard-fail on them — but a repo still wants the count to only go down. A warning ceiling gates CI truthfully while an existing docs tree is being adopted, without either lying about conformance or disabling the check. Directly relevant to lore's `check` gate, which has to stay honest about the spec's permissiveness while still being a gate.

adoption_candidates.feature: `--check-determinism`: a flag that re-runs generation and asserts byte-identical output
adoption_candidates.why: Determinism is lore's central claim, and by this repo's own gate doctrine a property never observed failing is not known to hold. A self-verifying flag converts the claim from prose into a negative control anyone can run, and it is exactly what catches an unordered map or a wall-clock timestamp leaking into output. okf-ingest's companion trick — making its one wall-clock field (ingested_at) overridable so fixtures stay byte-stable — is the practical way to keep such a check green honestly.

adoption_candidates.feature: Personalized-PageRank-ranked context assembly, with free-text-seeded multi-PPR when no start node is given
adoption_candidates.why: A context command that ranks by BFS depth pulls the wrong neighbours in a densely linked bundle — hop distance treats a hub index and a load-bearing decision doc identically. Exact PPR over the author-written link graph is deterministic, embedding-free, offline and cheap, so it upgrades ranking quality without giving up the no-LLM property. Keeping a rank='bfs' escape hatch preserves the old behaviour for comparison.

adoption_candidates.feature: Blast-radius guards on writes: a mutation declares how many documents and blocks it may touch, validated before anything is written, mandatory over MCP
adoption_candidates.why: lore is written to by agents, and the Story↔Task coupling means one bad write can desynchronise state across several files at once. A pre-write declared-scope check turns 'the agent edited more than it meant to' from a post-hoc git-diff discovery into a refused call that names the offending blocks. IWE making it non-optional over MCP is the right severity: the surface with the least human supervision gets the strictest contract.

adoption_candidates.feature: Atomic move with link healing — `mv` rewrites graph dependencies, relative body links and code references in one transaction
adoption_candidates.seen_in: open-doc-spec/ods (`ods mv <src> <dst>`); travisjakel/okf-ingest resolves [[wikilinks]] by name so links survive renames
adoption_candidates.why: Renaming a doc is the most common way a repo-resident bundle acquires dangling links, and lore's link-integrity gate only catches it after the damage. A move verb that rewrites every inbound reference prevents the class outright. For a tracker-coupled tool it must also rewrite the Backlog Task back-references — which no tool in this survey does, so it is a differentiator rather than a catch-up.

adoption_candidates.feature: `adopt` / `migrate`: scan a legacy non-conformant markdown tree and draft frontmatter as status: draft, bodies verbatim
adoption_candidates.seen_in: open-doc-spec/ods (`ods adopt <dir>`); serradura/okf-gem (`/okf migrate <path>` — 'adopted in place, bodies verbatim'); scaccogatto/okf-skills (`--migrate`, v0.1 `# Citations` → v0.2 `sources:`)
adoption_candidates.why: The adoption barrier for an OKF-native tool is an existing docs/ tree that is not OKF. Three tools solved it identically: deterministic in-place adoption that never rewrites prose, marking everything draft so the linter's completeness findings become the to-do list. The v0.1→v0.2 upgrade is the same shape and lore will need it regardless, since most of the ecosystem (okf-gem, openwiki, UmairBaig8/okf-generator) still emits v0.1.

adoption_candidates.feature: Derive trust tier and staleness at read time; never store them
adoption_candidates.seen_in: scaccogatto/okf-skills viewer; mandated by SPEC §5.3 (tiers derived from `verified`) and §5.1 (OKF records credibility SIGNALS, not a score)
adoption_candidates.why: Stated rationale: 'a stored tier is a stored opinion, and it goes stale.' This is a schema decision with teeth for lore: if `lore check` or a managed block ever writes a computed tier, freshness flag or health score into frontmatter, that value becomes a second source of truth that drifts from the verified/stale_after fields it was derived from — exactly the drift-is-a-defect failure this repo already guards against elsewhere. The same argument applies to any cached graph metric lore might persist.

adoption_candidates.feature: Impact analysis between two git refs, rendered as a sticky PR comment with `--fail-on-risk` merge gating
adoption_candidates.why: lore already has impact and snapshot verbs; what these add is the delivery surface — computing blast radius against a base ref without touching the working tree, then posting it as one updating comment rather than a new one per push. For a tracker-coupled tool the natural extension is naming which Backlog Tasks the changed Stories are coupled to, turning docs impact into delivery impact — a capability nothing in this survey has.

adoption_candidates.feature: A named bundle registry so a bundle is addressable from any directory (`okf registry set ./docs` → `@docs`)
adoption_candidates.seen_in: serradura/okf-gem (`okf registry`; a bare `okf server` hosts every registered bundle behind one hub); travisjakel/okf-mcp (`okf-mcp wiki=~/wiki notes=~/vault`)
adoption_candidates.why: Directly applicable to this estate's multi-repo problem. lore is repo-resident by design, but an agent in lore-cli routinely needs to read opum-doc's or saws's bundle to honour the fleet-routing rules. A per-user registry gives cross-bundle reads a stable address without teaching lore about remotes or weakening the repo-resident model, and the MCP-layer equivalent (named bundle arguments) makes the same addresses work for agents.

adoption_candidates.feature: Named, stable validation rule codes + bulk strict validation with a machine-readable report (`openspec validate --all --strict --json --concurrency <n>`)
adoption_candidates.why: OpenSpec's validator emits stable symbolic rule identifiers (REQUIREMENT_NO_SHALL, CHANGE_NO_DELTAS, DELTA_MISSING_REQUIREMENTS, SPEC_NO_REQUIREMENTS, CHANGE_SKIP_SPECS_CONFLICT, PURPOSE_TOO_BRIEF ...) rather than free-text messages. For lore this is the missing half of `lore check`: a JSON envelope carrying a stable rule code per finding lets a CI gate assert on specific failure classes and lets an agent branch on them deterministically, instead of regexing prose. The `--all` + `--concurrency` bulk mode is also the shape a repo-wide docs gate needs. Note OpenSpec still collapses everything to process exit 0/1 — lore's differentiated exit codes are strictly better, so adopt the rule-code vocabulary, not the exit model.

adoption_candidates.feature: A declarative workflow schema file that binds artifact ids -> output paths -> templates -> agent instructions -> `requires` dependency edges (`schemas/spec-driven/schema.yaml`)
adoption_candidates.why: OpenSpec externalizes its whole document pipeline into one versioned YAML (`name: spec-driven, version: 1`, then `artifacts: [{id, generates, description, template, instruction, requires}]`). That is a pluggable, data-driven answer to the same problem lore's OKF concept types solve in code, and it makes the artifact DAG (`requires`) declarative and inspectable. Directly relevant to LCLI-315 (pluggable tracker backends): the same pattern would let lore ship alternative doc workflows without recompiling, and it gives an obvious anchor for `lore graph` to traverse artifact-type edges, not just link edges.

adoption_candidates.feature: Working-set assembly as an explicit agent brief command with three renderings — JSON, human listing, and an editor workspace file (`openspec context [--json] [--code-workspace <path>]`)
adoption_candidates.why: `context` is the closest competitor analogue to lore's context command, and its design note is worth copying verbatim: 'Assembly is presentation over the relationship data; doctor is the health surface. The only write this command can perform is the explicitly requested workspace file.' That clean split — context never diagnoses, check never assembles, and context is read-only except for one opt-in write — is a good invariant for lore to state and gate. Worth noting as a competitive gap too: OpenSpec's context has no token budgeting at all, so a token-budgeted `lore context` is a genuine differentiator rather than table stakes.

adoption_candidates.feature: Write-time referential integrity on task->task dependencies, enforced with a nonzero exit (`backlog task create --dep TASK-999` -> exit 1, 'The following dependencies do not exist')
adoption_candidates.why: Verified empirically (without a pipe, so the code is the tool's): Backlog.md refuses to create a dangling task dependency and exits 1. But the adjacent `documentation:` frontmatter field is NOT checked — `backlog task create --doc docs/nope.md` succeeds with exit 0 and writes an unresolvable path. That asymmetry is precisely the seam lore couples across: Backlog.md guarantees the task->task edges, and nothing guarantees the task->doc edges. lore's link-integrity gate should treat every `documentation:` entry in every Backlog task as an in-scope edge (enumerated from the tracker, not from a curated list), because the tracker will never reject one.

adoption_candidates.feature: MCP server that advertises resources and prompts capabilities alongside tools, plus an instructions-retrieval tool (`get_backlog_instructions`) as tool #1 of 20
adoption_candidates.why: Probed over stdio: the server returns capabilities {tools:{listChanged}, resources:{listChanged}, prompts:{listChanged}, logging:{}} and 20 tools. Two things are worth copying for LCLI-42 (local lore MCP server). First, exposing docs as MCP *resources* rather than only tool calls lets a client page through the bundle without burning tool-call turns. Second, shipping the agent loop itself as a tool (`get_backlog_instructions`, mirroring `backlog instructions <guide>`) means the MCP client and the CLI agent read the same guidance from one source — which is exactly lore's `lore instructions <topic>` contract, and it should be an MCP tool too so the two surfaces cannot drift.

adoption_candidates.feature: Detect/repair split for graph integrity: `validate-dependencies` (report only) and `fix-dependencies` (auto-repair)
adoption_candidates.why: Task Master ships the diagnostic and the remediation as two separate commands, so CI can run the read-only one as a gate while a human or agent opts into the mutation. lore already has `lore check`; a sibling repair command with the same finding vocabulary would let the exit-6 drift gate stay strictly read-only and still offer a one-command fix. Caveat learned from probing it: Task Master's own error paths return exit 0 (a missing tasks.json printed an error and still exited 0), so copy the command split and explicitly not the exit-code behavior.

adoption_candidates.feature: A deterministic script layer that emits a JSON paths payload as the contract between the CLI and the LLM command templates (`scripts/bash/check-prerequisites.sh --json --require-tasks --include-tasks`, mirrored in PowerShell and Python)
adoption_candidates.why: Every spec-kit slash command declares, in its markdown frontmatter, the exact script invocation that feeds it: `scripts: {sh:..., ps:..., py:...}`. The script is deterministic and emits `{"FEATURE_DIR":"...","AVAILABLE_DOCS":[...]}`; the LLM only consumes that JSON. This is a clean, portable pattern for lore: it keeps the deterministic core auditable and testable in isolation while the agent-facing layer stays a thin prompt over a stable envelope. It also shows the frontmatter-declared-invocation idiom for generated skills, which would let `.claude/skills/lore/SKILL.md` name its own JSON entrypoints machine-readably.

adoption_candidates.feature: A one-way tasks -> GitHub Issues bridge driven by declared MCP tools (`/speckit.taskstoissues`, frontmatter `tools: ['github/github-mcp-server/list_issues','github/github-mcp-server/issue_write']`)
adoption_candidates.why: spec-kit declares, per command, exactly which external MCP tools it may call to push dependency-ordered tasks into GitHub Issues. For lore this is the shape of an export adapter under LCLI-315: the tracker-facing capability is declared as data (a tool allowlist) rather than hardcoded, which makes the blast radius reviewable and makes a Backlog.md-vs-other-tracker swap a config change. It is also a concrete competitive datapoint that spec-kit's issue coupling is LLM-mediated and one-way with no ID round-trip, so lore's deterministic, bidirectional Story<->Task IDs are a real differentiator.

adoption_candidates.feature: EARS-constrained requirement text with requirement IDs referenced from task items (`.kiro/specs/<feature>/requirements.md` -> `tasks.md`)
adoption_candidates.why: Kiro constrains requirement prose to a checkable grammar ('WHEN [condition] THE SYSTEM SHALL [behavior]') and has tasks cite requirement IDs, which makes AC-to-task traceability mechanically verifiable rather than a matter of reading. OpenSpec independently converged on the same idea with its REQUIREMENT_NO_SHALL rule. For lore, a lint that requires normative statements in Reference/Story concepts to match a SHALL-grammar, plus an ID-reference check from Backlog acceptance criteria back to the Story, would turn coverage from a dashboard into an exit-code gate. The layout is verified: a GitHub code search for path:.kiro/specs filename:requirements.md returned 32,448 hits, so this convention is widely established in real repos.

adoption_candidates.feature: Two independent time axes on every link: valid_at/invalid_at (world time) separate from created_at/expired_at (repo/system time)
adoption_candidates.why: This is the concrete answer to 'what does a temporal knowledge graph actually buy'. lore's snapshot/changed already gives transaction time essentially free and deterministically (content hashes over a git-resident tree — no LLM, unlike every tool here). What it CANNOT express is valid time: 'this API was deprecated as of 2026-03-01' is currently indistinguishable from 'someone edited the doc on 2026-03-01'. Adding an authored valid-interval to front matter (deprecated_at, superseded_at, effective_from) buys the second axis WITHOUT the LLM extraction that makes Graphiti non-deterministic, because the dates are declared by the author rather than inferred. Then `lore snapshot --as-of` can answer two genuinely different questions: what the contract was on date T, and what the repo said on date T.

adoption_candidates.feature: Invalidate-don't-delete with a supersession stamp taken from the superseding fact, not from wall-clock
adoption_candidates.why: When a new fact wins, Graphiti sets `edge.invalid_at = resolved_edge.valid_at` (valid-time end borrowed from the NEW fact) and `edge.expired_at = utc_now()` (transaction-time end), and never deletes. Applied to lore: superseding a Decision should stamp the old one with the successor's effective date, not the commit timestamp — otherwise the history reads as if the old decision held right up until someone got around to writing the new doc. This also makes 'what got superseded, by what, and when did it actually stop applying' a first-class query for `lore changed` rather than a diff the reader has to interpret.

adoption_candidates.feature: Out-of-order ingestion guard — a back-dated fact is born already expired
adoption_candidates.seen_in: Graphiti — edge_operations.py, the post-resolution block that sorts invalidation_candidates by valid_at and expires the NEW edge when a candidate is newer
adoption_candidates.why: Graphiti sorts candidates by valid_at and, if any candidate is newer than the incoming edge, sets `resolved_edge.invalid_at = candidate.valid_at; resolved_edge.expired_at = now` — the new edge enters the graph pre-expired. This is the single cheapest defence against a whole class of drift that a repo-resident tool is unusually exposed to: importing historical docs, restoring an old handover, or merging a long-lived branch must not silently reinstate superseded truth as current. A deterministic version is a few lines in the link resolver and turns a silent regression into a check failure with an exit code.

adoption_candidates.feature: Bidirectional provenance: source->derived as a first-class command, not just derived->source
adoption_candidates.seen_in: Graphiti — Graphiti.get_nodes_and_edges_by_episode() and MCP tool `get_episode_entities`; every EntityEdge also keeps an `episodes` uuid list
adoption_candidates.why: Graphiti makes episodes the ground-truth root and gives BOTH directions: an edge names the episodes that produced it, and one call inverts that to 'everything this source produced'. A provenance command that only resolves doc->source answers 'where did this claim come from'; the inverse answers 'this source file just changed — what in the bundle is now suspect', which is exactly impact analysis and is one call rather than a full-graph scan. Worth checking whether lore's impact command already covers the inverse or only the forward direction.

adoption_candidates.feature: Composable OR-of-ANDs date predicates over all four time columns, rather than a single --since flag
adoption_candidates.seen_in: Graphiti — SearchFilters in graphiti_core/search/search_filters.py (valid_at/invalid_at/created_at/expired_at as list[list[DateFilter]] with comparison operators including is_null)
adoption_candidates.why: A directly copyable query shape for lore's snapshot/changed surface. `--since` collapses to one axis and one operator; the OR-of-ANDs structure over four columns lets a caller express 'facts that became true before T but had not yet been recorded' or 'still-open intervals' (is_null on the end column) without new flags per question. It also serialises cleanly into a JSON envelope, so the MCP tool schema and the CLI flag surface can share one filter object instead of diverging.

adoption_candidates.feature: A minimum-viable temporal store that is ~200 lines of SQL and needs no LLM at all
adoption_candidates.seen_in: Mnemosyne — mnemosyne/core/triples.py (triples table with valid_from/valid_until; add() closes prior open rows; query(as_of=...))
adoption_candidates.why: Proof that the useful 80% of 'temporal knowledge graph' is cheap and fully deterministic: an interval per row, close-on-supersede, and `valid_from <= as_of AND (valid_until IS NULL OR valid_until > as_of)` for point-in-time reads. Graphiti buys the extra 20% (transaction time, contradiction detection, out-of-order handling) with two LLM calls per edge — a price a deterministic tool cannot pay. Also carries a free warning: Mnemosyne's own source records that keying auto-invalidation on (subject, predicate) silently destroyed multi-fact writes via add_facts(). Pick the invalidation key deliberately and test the multi-value case.

adoption_candidates.feature: Context budget enforced by the schema on assignment, not by truncation at render time
adoption_candidates.seen_in: Letta — letta/schemas/block.py: BaseBlock(validate_assignment=True) with `limit: int` and re-validation on every write to `value`
adoption_candidates.why: Letta's memory blocks declare a character limit that the Pydantic model enforces the moment the value changes, so an over-budget block is an error at write time with a stack trace, not a silently clipped context at read time. For a token-budgeted context command this is the difference between 'the agent quietly got two-thirds of the Story' and a check failure with a stable exit code naming the offending document. Budget belongs in the typed schema alongside the other front-matter constraints, and it should fail the gate — the character/token distinction is a detail; enforcement-at-write is the idea.

adoption_candidates.feature: A raw traversal escape hatch registered as a first-class query type alongside the curated ones
adoption_candidates.seen_in: cognee — SearchType.CYPHER plus cypher_search_retriever.py, one of 21 registered retrievers
adoption_candidates.why: Fixed graph verbs (path, impact, neighbours) cover the anticipated questions and hard-stop at the unanticipated one, which is when a user abandons the tool for grep and stops trusting the graph. cognee registers a raw Cypher retriever as just another search type. A deterministic analogue — a small declarative pattern/path expression evaluated over the resolved link graph, JSON envelope and exit codes unchanged — keeps ad-hoc queries inside the tool without weakening any guarantee, since nothing about determinism depends on the query surface being small.

adoption_candidates.feature: Deliberately tiny LLM-facing MCP surface (3 tools) with structured-JSON helpers kept separate
adoption_candidates.seen_in: cognee-mcp — remember / recall / forget as the only LLM-facing tools; list_datasets_json, list_dataset_data_json, create_dataset_json, get_client_info_json split off as UI/structured helpers
adoption_candidates.why: A useful counterweight to Graphiti's 13-tool MCP server. cognee splits the surface by AUDIENCE — three verbs the model is expected to reason about, and JSON helpers that exist for programmatic callers — rather than exposing every capability as a peer tool. For a docs+graph CLI whose command surface is large by design, that split is the design question worth settling explicitly: which commands does a model choose between, and which are merely callable. Every tool in the first group costs context and adds a wrong-tool failure mode on every turn.

adoption_candidates.feature: Binary-embedded, self-installing agent skill: `zetl skill init [--user|--global]` writes `.claude/skills/zetl/SKILL.md` from a copy compiled into the binary, so the on-disk skill carries the same version as the binary that wrote it and an upgrade plus re-run refreshes it
adoption_candidates.seen_in: zetl (and independently Logseq: `logseq skill show` / `skill install [--global]` writing `./.agents/skills/logseq-cli/SKILL.md`)
adoption_candidates.why: Two unrelated projects converged on this, which makes it a category expectation rather than a nicety. lore's skill at `.claude/skills/lore/SKILL.md` is hand-maintained in-repo, so it can silently describe a command surface the installed CLI no longer has — exactly the drift class this repo's CLAUDE.md treats as a defect. Emitting the skill from the binary makes skill/CLI drift structurally impossible, and `skill show` (print to stdout, always raw markdown even under `--output json`) is a cheap way to let CI diff the committed skill against the binary's and fail on mismatch.

adoption_candidates.feature: Three-way exit-code contract that separates tool failure from content failure: `0` success, `1` command error, `2` issues found — documented as a table per command, with the explicit note that `2` is the CI-friendly code
adoption_candidates.seen_in: Foam (`foam lint`, and the CLI's global exit-code table)
adoption_candidates.why: lore already has stable exit codes, but this specific split is the load-bearing part and is worth auditing lore against: CI must be able to distinguish "lore crashed / bad invocation" from "the docs bundle has integrity problems", because those demand different pipeline behaviour (retry-or-page vs. block-the-merge). Collapsing both into `1` produces the false-clear shape this repo's CLAUDE.md warns about, where a broken gate and a failing gate look identical.

adoption_candidates.feature: Time travel as a global flag rather than a subcommand: `--at "3 days ago"` is honoured by every read-only command, backed by silent jj-lib snapshots in `.zetl/jj/`, alongside `history log`, `history page <name>`, and temporal fields exposed to templates (`page.history`, `vault.history`, `page.backlinks[].since`)
adoption_candidates.why: lore has snapshot commands; making the temporal dimension an orthogonal global flag instead of a parallel command family means every future query command gets history for free and the JSON envelope shape stays identical whether you are reading now or reading last Tuesday. For an agent, that is the difference between learning one flag and learning a second set of commands. `page.backlinks[].since` is the sharpest detail — edge-level first-seen timestamps let you answer "what started depending on this Story, and when".

adoption_candidates.feature: Graph-level diff against a VCS ref with a category filter: `zetl diff --from <REF> | --since <DATE> --filter pages|links|orphans|dead-links`
adoption_candidates.why: This is impact analysis expressed as a diff rather than a traversal, and it is the natural CI primitive for a repo-resident tool: run it against the PR base and you get exactly the set of edges and orphans the branch introduced. It also makes a strictly-better gate than an absolute check — a repo with pre-existing dead links can still block *new* ones, which is how a link-integrity gate gets adopted into a codebase that is not already clean.

adoption_candidates.feature: Predicate vocabulary that emerges from the corpus and is only then frozen: typed edges `predicate::[[Target]]` with drift lints (`predicate-drift` flags low-frequency predicates near high-frequency ones as probable typos, `predicate-relates-to-overuse`, `predicate-undeclared-prefix`), promoted to hard enforcement by an optional `.zetl/predicates.toml` with `enforce = true`
adoption_candidates.why: This is a governance model, not a schema feature, and it solves the adoption problem a typed-edge system normally has: authors are never blocked by a vocabulary they have not designed yet, but once a team stabilises, an undeclared predicate becomes an ERROR and the file is the single pinned exemption set. That pinning property is exactly what this repo's CLAUDE.md demands of a gate — widening the vocabulary becomes a visible diff to a committed file rather than a silent drift. The deliberate omission is instructive too: the file carries no `inverse_of`, `transitive`, `domain`, or `range`, keeping the vocabulary declarative and pushing inference into a separate rules layer.

adoption_candidates.feature: Repo-committed saved queries surfaced as MCP tools: YAML descriptors under `.foam/queries/` exposed through `list_queries` (with match counts), `get_query`, and `run_query` (by saved `id` **or** an ad-hoc `descriptor`, exactly one)
adoption_candidates.why: This turns "the questions this repo's docs are meant to answer" into a versioned, reviewable artifact instead of prompt lore an agent has to rediscover each session. For lore it maps cleanly onto recurring Story/Task queries, and the `list_queries` match-count is the detail that makes it agent-usable — the agent can see which saved query is currently non-empty before spending a call running it. The one-of-two `id`-or-`descriptor` design also keeps the tool surface small while still allowing exploration.

adoption_candidates.feature: Per-tool and per-path scoped delegation tokens for MCP: `zetl delegate --tools search,get --scope "projects/**" --expiry 7d`, minting user-signed JWTs the server verifies, with `--allowed-issuer <DID>` restricting which identities may issue tokens for a given server
adoption_candidates.why: Foam's MCP server offers only a binary `mode: 'read' | 'read-write'`; zetl scopes by tool *and* by path glob *and* by expiry. For lore that is the difference between granting an agent the docs bundle and granting it one subtree of it — directly relevant to a fleet where multiple sessions and repos touch the same estate and where this repo's own guidance is that authority is per-concern rather than blanket.

adoption_candidates.feature: Typed refusal reasons on task-to-agent routing: `agent bridge` classifies each candidate task as `Routable` or `Not_routable of (Missing_stable_uuid | Missing_task_tag | Not_todo | Assignee_mismatch | Already_routed)`
adoption_candidates.why: The most directly transferable idea for lore's Story-to-Task coupling. Routing decisions usually get logged as prose or silently skipped; making non-routability a closed enum means an agent (or a human reading JSON) learns *why* a task was not picked up and can fix the specific defect — a missing stable id is a different action from an assignee mismatch. `Missing_stable_uuid` in particular is the failure mode a markdown-file-backed tracker hits constantly, and naming it as a first-class reason is what makes it fixable.

adoption_candidates.feature: Content-addressable Merkle blocks: `zetl blocks <page> --type heading|paragraph|spl|code|table|list|blockquote|frontmatter --resolve <BLAKE3-hash-or-prefix>`, addressable by hash prefix independent of the page
adoption_candidates.why: Gives every block a stable, position-independent identity, which is the missing primitive behind durable citation and transclusion: a reference survives the block moving between files, and `--resolve` by prefix means a provenance record can cite content rather than a line number that rots on the next edit. For a provenance-to-source command this is a strictly stronger anchor than file+line, and it composes with snapshot diffing — an unchanged hash proves a block did not change without re-reading it.

adoption_candidates.feature: Reasoning with explicit provenance and negative explanation: `reason explain <goal> --format natural|dot` (proof trees), `reason why-not <goal>` (explain unprovability), `reason require <goal> --assume "(fact)"` (what facts would suffice), `reason provenance <goal>` (trace to source file and line), `reason conflicts --suggest --fail-on-conflicts`
adoption_candidates.why: `why-not` and `require` are the genuinely novel pair — most tools can tell you what holds, almost none can tell you what is missing to make something hold, which is precisely the question an agent asks when a docs gate fails. `conflicts --fail-on-conflicts` is a second, orthogonal CI gate beyond link integrity: it fails the build when the documentation set contradicts itself, which is the machine-checkable version of the drift-is-a-defect rule this repo already enforces socially. Worth noting the whole engine is symbolic defeasible logic (SPL/Spindle Lisp), so it stays deterministic and offline — no LLM anywhere in the inference path.

adoption_candidates.feature: Watch mode as an event stream rather than a rebuild loop: `zetl watch --debounce <MS> --exec <CMD>` emits NDJSON graph events and pipes each event's JSON to a command on stdin
adoption_candidates.why: Makes incremental indexing composable — instead of lore owning every reaction to a docs change, downstream tooling subscribes to typed graph events (page added, link broken, orphan created). `--exec` receiving the event JSON on stdin is the detail that makes it usable without writing a plugin, and NDJSON keeps it greppable and jq-able in the same idiom as the rest of the JSON envelope.

adoption_candidates.feature: Split diagnostic severity from build-failure threshold: --log-level (what gets reported) and --log-failure-level (what fails the run) as independent axes, over JSON Lines output
adoption_candidates.why: lore currently couples 'this is a violation' to 'this exits non-zero'. Antora's split lets one CI job report everything at error level while a different job gates only at warn, without changing the tool or the rules. For lore's gate-design rule (a gate must report a real exit code and be provable by a negative control), an explicit failure-level dial makes the negative control trivial to run: set the threshold down, confirm the same finding now fails and names the path, set it back. JSONL also means findings are jq-filterable per-line rather than an all-or-nothing envelope.

adoption_candidates.feature: A published, machine-readable cross-reference inventory (objects.inv) keyed by domain and object type, inspectable with a one-line command
adoption_candidates.why: This is the missing primitive for cross-repository linking in a fleet of repo-resident bundles. If each repo's lore bundle emitted a typed inventory of its concepts (adr:*, spec:*, story:*, runbook:*, reference:*) as a build artifact, another repo's `lore check` could resolve and validate outbound cross-repo links deterministically and offline, with no server and no API. Sphinx has run this exact federation model for two decades; the inspection command (python -m sphinx.ext.intersphinx <url>) is what makes a broken cross-repo link debuggable instead of mysterious.

adoption_candidates.feature: A link checker that writes output.json alongside human output AND sets process exit status 1
adoption_candidates.why: Direct precedent for lore's JSON-envelope-plus-stable-exit-code contract, and proof the two are not in tension: emit the human report and the machine report from the same pass, then set the code. Note the specific trap it avoids, which lore's own CLAUDE.md already names — the status is set on the app object during the build rather than derived from a downstream pipe, so `tool | tail` can never launder a failure into a pass.

adoption_candidates.feature: nitpick_ignore / nitpick_ignore_regex: a pinned exemption set of (warning_type, target) tuples for known-missing references
adoption_candidates.why: lore's gate doctrine requires exemptions to be individually justified and pinned so widening the set is a visible failure. Sphinx's form is the proven shape: exemptions are typed pairs, not path globs, so an exemption for one dangling reference cannot silently cover a different one that appears later. The regex variant shows how to keep it usable at scale without degrading into a directory-scoped allowlist — the exact anti-pattern lore's rules call a hand-scoped list in an enumeration costume.

adoption_candidates.feature: Emitting JSON Schema for your own content collections (.astro/collections/<name>.schema.json) generated from the authoring schema
adoption_candidates.why: lore owns a closed typed-concept system but the type definitions live inside the binary. Emitting a JSON Schema per concept type into the bundle makes the contract consumable by editors, by CI in other languages, by a task tracker validating Story frontmatter, and by an agent that needs to know what fields a Runbook requires before authoring one — without shelling out to lore. It also converts 'what is a valid ADR' from tribal knowledge into a diffable artifact, which is what makes drift between lore-cli and a *-doc owner detectable rather than arguable.

adoption_candidates.feature: Per-diagnostic severity tree: validation.{nav,links}.{not_found,anchors,absolute_links,unrecognized_links} each independently warn|info|ignore
adoption_candidates.why: A single --strict flag forces one policy on every class of breakage, so teams disable the whole gate to tolerate one nuisance class. A severity tree lets lore keep dangling typed links fatal while a missing anchor or an absolute link stays informational, which is the difference between a gate teams keep on and a gate they switch off. Pair it with Docusaurus' choice of defaults — the link class defaults to throw while anchors default to warn — so the strictest setting is the one that ships.

adoption_candidates.feature: A machine-readable verdict paired with a semantic exit code: `fern diff --from-version` prints JSON with the computed bump and next version, exiting non-zero when the bump is major
adoption_candidates.why: This is the closest existing analogue to lore's impact command, and it resolves the design question of what an impact/diff command should return. Not a report — a verdict object plus an exit code whose meaning is the verdict, so a pre-merge hook can act on the code alone while a human or agent reads the JSON for the why. Fern also demonstrates the local-versus-live split lore needs: `fern check`'s broken-links rule resolves against the local navigation tree (deterministic, offline, pre-commit) while `fern docs link check` crawls a published site (network, post-deploy) — two different commands rather than one command with a flag.

adoption_candidates.feature: Auto-regenerated skill.md hosted alongside the docs and exposed as an MCP resource, consolidating capabilities, limitations and best practices that documentation scatters across pages
adoption_candidates.why: lore already ships .claude/skills/lore/SKILL.md by hand, which is a drift surface: the skill describes a command surface that the binary owns. Generating the skill from the bundle and the command registry on every docs change makes the skill unable to disagree with what ships — the same argument this repo makes for managed blocks. Mintlify's second move is the one to copy exactly: serve the skill as an MCP *resource* rather than only as a file, so an agent that connects to the bundle discovers how to use it without a separate install step.

adoption_candidates.feature: Page-scoped context endpoints: append /llms.txt to any page URL for a page-level index, or .md for that page's markdown; site-level llms.txt hard-capped at 100,000 characters with explicit truncation
adoption_candidates.why: lore's context command needs a defensible budgeting story, and these two show both halves. Fern's scoping means an agent asks for context about one node rather than the whole bundle — the natural companion to lore's graph/path commands, where the traversal picks the nodes and the scoped endpoint materializes just those. Mintlify's explicit character cap with declared truncation is the honest failure mode: a budget that is documented and enforced beats one that silently overflows a context window. Mintlify's Link: rel="llms-txt" and X-Llms-Txt headers are the discovery convention if lore ever serves the bundle over HTTP.

adoption_candidates.feature: Per-page git provenance computed from content-source origin: {web_url}, {refname}, {reftype}, {refhash}, {path} placeholders resolved for every page
adoption_candidates.why: Most tools' provenance is a static edit_uri template that says which file a page came from. Antora resolves the commit hash and ref type per page, so provenance identifies a point in history rather than a moving branch. For lore, where a Reference's claim must trace to the artifact that justified it, the refhash is the difference between a citation that stays true and one that silently becomes wrong when the source file changes — the same failure this repo's own authoring rules describe as a transcription going stale.

adoption_candidates.feature: `mint score`: a 29-check agent-navigation readiness grade, runnable against your own site or an arbitrary URL
adoption_candidates.why: lore validates correctness (schemas, links, coupling) but has no measure of agent-readiness — whether the bundle is actually navigable by an agent that has never seen it. A deterministic `lore score` over checkable properties (every concept reachable from an entry point, every typed edge bidirectional, no orphan nodes, description density, stable anchors) turns a quality argument into a number that can regress in CI. Scoring an arbitrary target is the second half: it makes the metric falsifiable by letting you run it against docs bundles you did not author.

adoption_candidates.feature: A programmatic content catalog exposed to extensions: contentCatalog.findBy(query), getPages(filter), resolvePage(spec, context), getComponentVersion(name, version)
adoption_candidates.why: Antora's model is component/version/module/page with typed file families, and extensions query it as a graph — evidence that a docs graph query API is viable and useful, and a source of naming for lore's own surface. The gap it leaves is the opportunity: this is an in-process JavaScript API available only to extension authors during a build, with no CLI equivalent, so nothing outside a build can ask a question about the graph. lore exposing the equivalent as commands with JSON envelopes is a genuine differentiator rather than a reimplementation.

adoption_candidates.feature: Emit AGENTS.md as the primary agent-instruction artifact AND a CLAUDE.md whose first line is `@AGENTS.md` — do not choose between them, and do not emit AGENTS.md alone
adoption_candidates.why: Direct answer to the brief: AGENTS.md is the convergence point (60,000+ OSS projects; LF/Agentic AI Foundation stewardship since 2025-12-09; read by Codex, Cursor, Devin, Copilot, VS Code, Gemini CLI, Amp, Factory, Jules, Junie, goose, opencode, Zed, Warp and more) but Claude Code is explicitly NOT a reader: "Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md`, not `AGENTS.md`." A deterministic docs CLI is exactly the right thing to own this bridge, because the two-file form is the documented, vendor-blessed one and hand-maintaining it drifts. Generate `CLAUDE.md` as `@AGENTS.md` plus a Claude-specific tail (lore loop, `lore instructions`), and prefer the import over `ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md` since the symlink cannot carry Claude-specific content and needs Administrator or Developer Mode on Windows. Both files should be managed blocks so `lore check` can gate their staleness.

adoption_candidates.feature: Budget the generated AGENTS.md against Codex's `project_doc_max_bytes` (32 KiB default) and its root-to-leaf concatenation order
adoption_candidates.why: Codex builds one instruction chain per run: `~/.codex/AGENTS.override.md` or `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`, then every directory from project root down to cwd (checking AGENTS.override.md, AGENTS.md, then project_doc_fallback_filenames), concatenated with blank lines, and it "stops adding files once the combined size reaches the limit." A generator that emits a large root AGENTS.md silently starves the nested per-package files below it — a failure with no error message anywhere. This is a hard, checkable number: `lore check` should fail when the emitted AGENTS.md set would exceed 32 KiB, and report the byte budget in its JSON envelope. It also argues for emitting small nested AGENTS.md files per docs subtree rather than one root monolith, which both Codex and Cursor resolve closest-wins.

adoption_candidates.feature: Write the generated skill to the vendor-neutral `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` path in addition to `.claude/skills/`
adoption_candidates.seen_in: Cursor skills docs + Agent Skills spec
adoption_candidates.why: Cursor's documented load order lists `.agents/skills/` and `~/.agents/skills/` first, with `.claude/skills/` and `.codex/skills/` explicitly framed as compatibility paths. Emitting to `.agents/skills/` makes one generated skill first-class in Cursor, Codex, Copilot/VS Code, Gemini CLI, opencode, goose, Amp, Factory, Junie, Roo Code and Kiro without a per-vendor emitter, while a symlink or duplicate at `.claude/skills/` preserves Claude Code (which follows symlinks and de-duplicates when the same target is reachable from more than one location).

adoption_candidates.feature: Restrict generated SKILL.md frontmatter to the spec's six fields and gate it with a `validate` command modeled on `skills-ref validate`
adoption_candidates.why: The spec's constraints are mechanically checkable and lore already owns deterministic validation with exit codes: name 1-64 chars, lowercase a-z/0-9/hyphen, no leading/trailing/consecutive hyphens, must match the parent directory name; description 1-1024 non-empty; compatibility <=500; metadata a string->string map; allowed-tools space-separated. Anything beyond {name, description, license, compatibility, metadata, allowed-tools} is rejected on the claude.ai/Skills API path with "Unexpected key(s) in SKILL.md frontmatter". A lore-generated bridge that quietly emits a seventh key produces a skill that loads in Claude Code but fails everywhere else — precisely the silent-drift class of defect lore exists to catch. The reference implementation is self-described as demonstration-only, so a production-grade validator with a stable JSON envelope and exit code is an open niche, not a duplicated one.

adoption_candidates.feature: Adopt the Agent Skills progressive-disclosure numbers as the published contract for `lore context`
adoption_candidates.why: The spec states real numbers rather than vibes: metadata ~100 tokens loaded at startup for every skill, full SKILL.md body <5000 tokens recommended and <500 lines, resources loaded only on demand, file references kept one level deep from SKILL.md. A token-budgeted context command is more credible and more testable when it commits to a comparable published tier structure (index tier / body tier / on-demand tier) and reports actual token counts in its JSON envelope, and it makes lore's generated skills conformant by construction rather than by review.

adoption_candidates.feature: A repo-resident, hard-capped generation-steering file in the shape of `.devin/wiki.json`
adoption_candidates.why: Cognition's steering file is a good precedent precisely because its limits are numeric and enforced rather than advisory: `repo_notes` capped at 10,000 characters per note and 100 notes total, `pages` capped at 30 with unique non-empty titles and optional parent relationships, and an explicit override semantic ("If `pages` is provided, we'll bypass the default cluster-based planning"). For a deterministic OKF CLI the transferable parts are the validated caps and the author-override escape hatch — caps that fail loudly at generation time are the difference between a config file and a gate, and the parent-relationship field is a plain-JSON way to declare hierarchy that lore's graph could emit and re-ingest.

adoption_candidates.feature: Structure-before-content MCP tool triad, mirroring `read_wiki_structure` / `read_wiki_contents` / `ask_question`
adoption_candidates.why: DeepWiki's free public MCP server ships only three tools, and the ordering is the design: an agent lists topics first, then reads only what it needs, and only then asks a grounded question. That maps cleanly onto lore's existing graph/read/context split and is worth matching in tool naming and description text so agents that have learned the DeepWiki idiom transfer to lore's server without prompting. It is also the competitive contrast to state plainly: DeepWiki's answers are LLM-generated and non-reproducible, whereas lore's equivalent triad can be deterministic with stable exit codes — the same shape, with a guarantee attached.

adoption_candidates.feature: Emit `docs/llms.txt` (v2) plus `.md` mirrors with `rel="alternate"` / `rel="describedby"` discovery links
adoption_candidates.why: Cheap for a tool that already owns the docs tree, and it is the one artifact in this category that is both deterministically parseable and consumed off-repo: the spec fixes section order (H1 name, blockquote summary, non-heading prose, H2 file lists of `[name](url): notes`), placement at any subpath with most-specific-wins, Chrome Lighthouse audits for it, and OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini all publish one. lore's Story/Reference graph already has the titles, summaries and edges the format wants. Two details worth copying beyond the file itself: the `## Optional` section as a documented "skip this under a tighter budget" tier, which is a cleaner two-tier budget signal than a token count; and the `Link:` HTTP header form of the discovery relations, which lets a published docs site advertise its markdown mirrors from CDN config without touching pages.

adoption_candidates.feature: Path-scoped instruction emission via `.claude/rules/` `paths:` frontmatter and nested AGENTS.md
adoption_candidates.why: Both major readers now support deferring instructions until an agent touches matching files — Claude Code via YAML `paths:` globs on `.claude/rules/*.md` (bounded at 1,000 expanded patterns / 4 MiB per rule), Cursor via `globs` in `.mdc` and via nested AGENTS.md with closest-file-wins. A docs CLI that knows which Stories and References cover which source paths can emit path-scoped rules automatically, which is something a human maintaining these files by hand essentially never does. It also directly relieves the 32 KiB Codex budget pressure above by moving per-area guidance out of the root file.

adoption_candidates.feature: Non-vacuity encoded as its own exit code (32 = 'the extractor didn't find any code to analyze')
adoption_candidates.why: This repo's CLAUDE.md requires that a gate 'assert non-vacuity, so an empty or mis-globbed run fails instead of passing' and warns that a green gate reads as proof - 'the most confident possible false clear'. CodeQL turns that requirement into a machine-readable outcome rather than a convention: a run that matched nothing exits 32, distinguishable by a caller from both success (0) and error (2). lore's check/validate/graph commands should reserve a dedicated code for 'the scan matched zero documents', so a mis-scoped glob in CI fails loudly instead of certifying an empty corpus. CodeQL also separates exit 1 ('the answer to your question is no') from exit 2 ('something went wrong'), which is the distinction a scripting caller actually needs and which most tools here collapse.

adoption_candidates.feature: Corpus fingerprint on every response, with pagination cursors bound to it and a typed invalid-cursor outcome
adoption_candidates.why: Every substantive MCP response carries `corpusHealth { fingerprint, recordCount, excludedCount }`, and cursors are bound to both that fingerprint and the query shape, so resuming a walk against a changed corpus returns a non-error `invalid-cursor` outcome naming the reason (`corpus-changed`, `query-mismatch`, `wrong-channel`, `offset-out-of-range`, `cursor-not-applicable`, `version-unsupported`, `decode-failed`) rather than silently mixing pages from two states. lore already has snapshot and provenance; adding a bundle fingerprint to every JSON envelope makes an agent's multi-call session verifiable, lets a cached answer be invalidated correctly, and turns 'the docs changed under me mid-task' from an invisible corruption into a typed, recoverable event. `recordCount` in the same object doubles as the non-vacuity signal above.

adoption_candidates.feature: Federated cross-repository refs that are INERT when the foreign log has no snapshot, rather than dangling
adoption_candidates.why: A ref of the form `<log>:<id>` resolves against a supplied federated-log snapshot; if that log has no snapshot supplied, the ref classifies as `federated-absent` and is inert - explicitly never an orphan failure - while a local unresolvable ref is still a hard `dangling` error, and status precedence keeps the dangling failure ranked above the inert one. This is exactly the problem this repo has: CLAUDE.md requires citing `opum-ai/opum-doc` and `saws` as owners of concerns lore-cli does not own, but lore's link-integrity gate cannot resolve into a private peer repo. Today that forces either an untracked prose citation or a gate exemption. A three-way classification (resolved / dangling / foreign-log-absent) lets lore represent a cross-repo citation as a first-class typed edge that the gate deliberately declines to fail on, without weakening the local dangling-link check - and CLAUDE.md's own rule about pinning exemption sets is satisfied because the inertness is derived from an absent snapshot, not a hand-maintained ignore list.

adoption_candidates.feature: Bidirectional docs-to-code binding: `affects` glob/package matchers on the doc plus `@adr NNNN` opt-in markers in source, with `explain <path>` reporting which route fired
adoption_candidates.why: A record declares the globs it governs, and any source file can additionally opt in with a one-line comment marker in any language with no schema change - so `affects` stays narrow (the defining files) while the surrounding code opts in incrementally. `adr explain <path>` then prints not just which decisions govern a file but WHY, keeping the two routes visually distinct (`via path: src/**` versus `declared by src/sync.ts:3`), and only `accepted` records count as governing while matched proposals and superseded records are listed separately. lore's impact and provenance commands run over docs; this is the missing inverse - given a changed source file, which docs govern it - and it is the join that makes a docs graph useful in a PR gate. The CI Action that comments governing decisions on PRs is the delivery vehicle, and it degrades rather than failing on a read-only fork token.

adoption_candidates.feature: Impact scoped to a git range, with mutually-implied flags enforced by the parser
adoption_candidates.why: `--untracked`, `--uncommitted`, `--files`, `--base` and `--head` are each declared with yargs `.implies(..., 'affected')`, so none can be supplied without `--affected`; `--json` and `--sep` are declared `.conflicts()` in both directions. The incoherent invocation is unrepresentable rather than validated after parse, which is the same 'make the gate structurally sound, not conventionally sound' discipline CLAUDE.md demands of prose. Substantively, `--base`/`--head` (plus `NX_BASE`/`NX_HEAD`) are the right shape for lore's impact command: blast radius is almost always asked about a diff, not about the whole tree. Nx's `DependencyType.static | dynamic | implicit` is also worth mirroring as an edge kind, to separate a real markdown link from a declared Story/Task coupling in the same graph.

adoption_candidates.feature: Per-tool hard caps with declared truncation behaviour, and oversize handled by exclusion-plus-finding rather than silent truncation
adoption_candidates.seen_in: Sourcebot MCP (caps on every tool) and adrkit (64 KiB per-record cap)
adoption_candidates.why: Sourcebot documents a numeric bound and its truncation semantics on every single tool - `read_file` offset plus limit at max 500 lines, `list_tree` depth 1-10 and maxEntries max 10000 default 1000, `grep`/`glob` limit default 100, page/perPage max 100 - so an agent can plan a walk instead of discovering a cap by hitting it. adrkit supplies the complementary half: an oversized record is EXCLUDED and reported as a `record-too-large` finding, 'never truncated', and the exclusion count rides along in `corpusHealth.excludedCount`. For lore's `context` command that pairing is the correct contract - a silently truncated doc is worse than an omitted one, because the agent cannot tell it read half a decision.

adoption_candidates.feature: An MCP surface shaped as a generate -> validate -> run loop for agent-authored queries, shipped with the skill that scripts it
adoption_candidates.why: Both tools concluded that an agent writing a query needs to debug it before running it. ast-grep exposes `dump_syntax_tree(format=cst|ast|pattern)` so the agent can see how the tool parses both the target code AND its own candidate pattern, then `test_match_code_rule` to check a rule against a snippet before it touches the repo - and ships `ast-grep.mdc` codifying the five-step loop, with a deliberately instructive error on no-match. adg's MCP serves `get_dsl_reference` (the full grammar on demand) plus `list_rule_files` (in-repo examples as few-shot material) and `validate_rule`. lore has `query`, `traversal` and `agents`/`agent` profiles but no MCP server at all - the largest single gap against this landscape, since adrkit, adg, ast-grep, Nx, Sourcebot and CodeQL all have one. If lore adds one, this dry-run-then-execute shape is the pattern to adopt rather than a bare search endpoint.

adoption_candidates.feature: Monikers - a two-stage local-id then ecosystem-id scheme for joining independently produced graphs
adoption_candidates.why: This is the only mechanism found in the whole survey that directly addresses 'can a docs graph be joined to a code graph'. LSIF emits language-internal symbol ids, then a separate pass (`lsif tsc --stdout | lsif npm --stdin --package package.json --stdout`) rewrites them into stable npm-ecosystem monikers, deliberately keeping the two stages separable so the ids can be inspected between them. Neither side has to own the other's namespace and neither has to be regenerated when the other changes. If lore ever wants a doc node to reference a code symbol, minting a stable external identifier as a distinct, inspectable step is the design - and SCIP's explicit refusal to be queryable ('a transmission format ... not a storage format for querying', with 'Avoid direct encoding of graphs' as a core design decision) confirms the join has to be lore's own layer, not something a code indexer will hand over.

adoption_candidates.feature: Derived predicates materialized into the database, plus incrementality by stacking databases
